reviews.note: The formation, relative-time explanation, examples, readings, translations, and correction are accurate; the level is plausible.

entries.title: After doing something, then…
entries.meaning: V-てから Y: after V, Y; also, since V.
entries.when: Use it to say one action comes first and another follows it, especially when the order matters: wash your hands, then eat; finish homework, then go out. A second common use counts time from an event: 日本に来てから一年, “a year since I came to Japan”. ～たあとで also means “after”, and the two often overlap; ～てから tends to stress that the first action is done first, while ～たあとで tends to focus on the time that follows.
entries.why: から marks a starting point. After a verb’s て-form, it sets an earlier event or situation as the starting point for what follows: 洗ってから is “starting from having washed”. In a sequence of actions, the first is normally finished before the next begins. In the “since” use, the starting point can be the beginning of a situation that is still going on: 東京に住んでから、もう十年になります. The tense and politeness go on the final verb, not on the て-form. After a plain form such as 帰った, から means “because” instead, so the form before から decides the meaning.

formation.note: Tense and politeness go on the main clause: 食べてから出かけました.

formation.form: V (て-form) + から + length of time
formation.note: Time since: 来てから三年.

examples.japanese: 手を洗ってから、ご飯を食べます。
examples.reading: てをあらってから、ごはんをたべます。
examples.romaji: te o aratte kara, gohan o tabemasu.
examples.english: I wash my hands, then eat.

examples.japanese: 宿題をしてから、遊びに行きました。
examples.reading: しゅくだいをしてから、あそびにいきました。
examples.romaji: shukudai o shite kara, asobi ni ikimashita.
examples.english: I did my homework and then went out to play.

examples.reading: にほんにきてから、いちねんになります。
examples.romaji: nihon ni kite kara, ichinen ni narimasu.

mistake.wrong: 家に帰ったから、テレビを見ました。
mistake.problem: Meant as “after I got home”. But から after a plain past verb means “because”, so this says “Because I got home, I watched TV”. For “after”, から follows the て-form.
mistake.right: 家に帰ってから、テレビを見ました。

distinguish_from.note: から after a plain form (帰ったから) gives a reason. から after the て-form (帰ってから) gives an order in time.
～てから: V first, then the main action. ～まえに: the main action first, before V.
～たり～たりする lists sample actions in no particular order; ～てから fixes the order.

review.note: The contrast with ～たあとで is kept short and stated as a tendency; あとで has no OJG id in the N5 list, so it is only in `when`. Please confirm the time-since use belongs at N5; ～になる in the third example is OJG-0028 (N5).

reviews.note: The explanation, formation, examples, readings, translations, and contrasts are accurate. The mistake correctly distinguishes causal 帰ったから from temporal 帰ってから, and N5 is a plausible level.

The meaning and reasoning overstate completion: ～てから does not always mean that V has finished. In its “since” use, it can establish the beginning of an ongoing situation: 東京に住んでから、もう十年になります means “It has already been ten years since I started living in Tokyo,” without implying that the residence ended. Replace the meaning with “V-てから Y: after V, Y; also, since V.” Replace the first two sentences of the reasoning with “から marks a starting point. After a verb’s て-form, it establishes an earlier event or situation as the starting point for what follows. In action sequences, the first action is normally completed before the next begins; in the ‘since’ use, the starting point can be the beginning of a situation that continues.” The examples and their translations are correct.
The explanation, formation, examples, and contrasts are accurate.

entries.title: Giving reasons, and there may be more
entries.meaning: Plain form + し: lines up one or more reasons or points, hinting there are others; often leads to a conclusion.
entries.when: Use it to list reasons or features that add up to a conclusion: この店は安いし、おいしいし、よく来ます, "this shop is cheap, and it's good, so I come often". A single し gives one reason and suggests it is not the only one. When the conclusion is obvious, it can be left unsaid: 今日は忙しいし… is a gentle way of saying no.
entries.why: し adds a point to a pile. Each clause before it is a complete statement, so it keeps its own tense and negation (高いし, 高くないし, 雨だったし), and a noun or な-adjective needs だ to be a statement at all (静かだし). Because the points are piled up to support one conclusion, they normally all point the same way: all reasons for, or all reasons against. And because a pile can always hold more, even one し sounds like "for one thing", which makes it softer than から. から presents the cause; し offers supporting evidence.

formation.note: 行くし, 行かないし, 行ったし; 高いし, 高くないし. In polite speech, polite forms also occur before し: 行きますし.
学生だし, 静かだし; past 雨だったし. The だ cannot be left out.

examples.reading: このへやはひろいし、えきからちかいし、とてもいいです。
examples.romaji: kono heya wa hiroi shi, eki kara chikai shi, totemo ii desu.
examples.english: This room is spacious, and it's close to the station; it's really good.

examples.japanese: 今日は雨だし、寒いし、うちにいます。
examples.reading: きょうはあめだし、さむいし、うちにいます。
examples.romaji: kyō wa ame da shi, samui shi, uchi ni imasu.
examples.english: It's raining today, and it's cold, so I'm staying home.

examples.japanese: もう遅いし、そろそろ帰ります。
examples.reading: もうおそいし、そろそろかえります。
examples.romaji: mō osoi shi, sorosoro kaerimasu.
examples.english: It's late, for one thing, so I'll be heading home.

mistake.wrong: この町は静かし、きれいだし、大好きです。
mistake.problem: A な-adjective needs だ before し, because each item has to be a complete statement. 静か on its own is not one.
mistake.right: この町は静かだし、きれいだし、大好きです。

distinguish_from.note: から states the reason as the cause of what follows. し offers one or more reasons as supporting points and leaves room for more, so it sounds less absolute.

entries.title: I hear that… (passing on what you heard)
entries.meaning: Plain form + そうです: reports something the speaker heard or read, "I hear that…", "apparently".
entries.when: Use it to pass on information that came from someone else, the news, a notice: 明日は雨が降るそうです, "I hear it's going to rain tomorrow". The source can be named first with によると: 天気予報によると.
entries.why: そう means "so, like that", and here it points back at a statement: "it is said so". Because it attaches to a complete statement, everything before it keeps its own tense and negation (降った, 降らない), and a noun or な-adjective keeps its だ (雨だそうです). The そうです itself does not change: the point is always "that is what I heard", so it has no past form of its own in this use, and it is not made negative to deny the report. Saying where the information came from matters in Japanese: this form marks the content as not your own knowledge.

formation.form: Verb / い-adjective (plain form, any tense) + そうです
formation.note: 降るそうです, 降ったそうです, 降らないそうです; 高いそうです. Casual: そうだ.

formation.form: Noun / な-adjective + だ + そうです
formation.note: 雨だそうです, 静かだそうです; past 雨だったそうです.

examples.japanese: 天気予報によると、明日は雨が降るそうです。
examples.reading: てんきよほうによると、あしたはあめがふるそうです。
examples.romaji: tenki yohō ni yoru to, ashita wa ame ga furu sō desu.
examples.english: According to the weather forecast, it's going to rain tomorrow.

examples.japanese: 田中さんは来月結婚するそうです。
examples.reading: たなかさんはらいげつけっこんするそうです。
examples.romaji: tanaka-san wa raigetsu kekkon suru sō desu.
examples.english: I hear Tanaka-san is getting married next month.

examples.japanese: あの店のラーメンはとてもおいしいそうです。
examples.reading: あのみせのラーメンはとてもおいしいそうです。
examples.romaji: ano mise no rāmen wa totemo oishii sō desu.
examples.english: I hear the ramen at that shop is really good.

mistake.wrong: ニュースによると、明日はとても寒そうです。
mistake.problem: 寒そう, the adjective stem + そう, gives the speaker's own impression from what they see. A report from the news needs the full plain form before そうです.
mistake.right: ニュースによると、明日はとても寒いそうです。

distinguish_from.note: The "looks like" そうです attaches to a stem (降りそう, 寒そう) and gives your own impression. The hearsay そうです attaches to a full plain form (降るそう, 寒いそう) and passes on what you heard.

review.note: Tanos lists そうです (486) and ～そうです (505) separately; this entry takes 486 as the hearsay use, since Hanabira's ～そうだ was mapped to 0061 as "looks like". Is that the right split?

entries.title: Try doing something to see how it goes
entries.meaning: V-てみる: do V to see what it is like or what happens; "try V-ing".
entries.when: Use it when you do something as an experiment, or for the first time, to find out the result: 着てみる, "try it on"; 食べてみる, "try eating it". It is common in requests (聞いてみてください) and wishes (行ってみたい).
entries.why: みる is "see, look". After the て-form it says "do V, and see": you carry out the action, then look at how it turns out. So the action really is done; てみる is not an attempt that can fail. For "tried to, but could not", Japanese uses a different form (V-ようとした). Because the point is to find something out, てみる suits new and unfamiliar things. As a helper verb, みる is normally written in kana.

formation.note: Polite: てみます. Wish: てみたい. Request: てみてください.

examples.japanese: この靴をはいてみてもいいですか。
examples.reading: このくつをはいてみてもいいですか。
examples.romaji: kono kutsu o haite mite mo ii desu ka.
examples.english: May I try these shoes on?

examples.japanese: 初めて納豆を食べてみました。
examples.reading: はじめてなっとうをたべてみました。
examples.romaji: hajimete nattō o tabete mimashita.
examples.english: I tried natto for the first time.

examples.japanese: わからないときは、先生に聞いてみてください。
examples.reading: わからないときは、せんせいにきいてみてください。
examples.romaji: wakaranai toki wa, sensei ni kiite mite kudasai.
examples.english: When you don't understand, try asking the teacher.

mistake.wrong: 早く起きてみましたが、起きられませんでした。
mistake.problem: てみる means the action was actually done to see the result, so "tried getting up, but couldn't get up" contradicts itself. An attempt that failed is V-ようとした.
mistake.right: 早く起きようとしましたが、起きられませんでした。

entries.title: If it's that…, if that's the case
entries.meaning: X なら: "if it's X", "if (as you say) X"; takes up something given and says what applies to it.
entries.when: Use it to respond to something just said or to the situation, with advice, a suggestion or an opinion about it: 京都に行くなら、秋がいいですよ, "if you're going to Kyoto, autumn is good". After a noun, it picks that thing out as the topic of what you are about to say: 駅なら、あそこです, "the station? it's over there".
entries.why: なら takes something as given, usually from the listener or the context, and then says what follows if that is so. It only sets up the premise; it says nothing about which happens first. That is why the second part can come before the first in time: in 京都に行くなら、ガイドブックを買ったほうがいい, you buy the guidebook before you go. たら and と need the first event to happen first, and なら does not, which makes it the natural choice for advice about someone's plan.

formation.note: 駅なら, 静かなら.
行くなら, 行かないなら, 行ったなら; 寒いなら. のなら and, in speech, んなら also occur.

examples.japanese: 京都に行くなら、秋がいいですよ。
examples.reading: きょうとにいくなら、あきがいいですよ。
examples.romaji: kyōto ni iku nara, aki ga ii desu yo.
examples.english: If you're going to Kyoto, autumn is a good time.

examples.japanese: 「駅はどこですか。」「駅なら、あそこです。」
examples.reading: 「えきはどこですか。」「えきなら、あそこです。」
examples.romaji: "eki wa doko desu ka." "eki nara, asoko desu."
examples.english: "Where is the station?" "The station? It's over there."

examples.japanese: 寒いなら、窓を閉めましょうか。
examples.reading: さむいなら、まどをしめましょうか。
examples.romaji: samui nara, mado o shimemashō ka.
examples.english: If you're cold, shall I close the window?

mistake.wrong: 駅に着くなら、電話してください。
mistake.problem: The call should come after arriving. なら does not set an order, so this reads as "if you are going to arrive, call me", possibly beforehand. For "when you have arrived, then call", use たら.
mistake.right: 駅に着いたら、電話してください。

distinguish_from.note: たら says B happens once A has happened. なら takes A as given and says what applies, whatever the order in time.

entries.title: How many times in a period
entries.meaning: Period + に + count: "so many times per period", as in 一週間に三回, "three times a week".
entries.when: Use it to say how often something happens within a length of time: 一日に三回, "three times a day"; 一か月に一度, "once a month". The period comes first, then に, then the number of times.
entries.why: に marks the frame an action is placed in. Here the frame is a length of time, and the count says how many times the action fits into it. The count is a quantity, and like other quantities it sits just before the verb with no particle of its own: 一週間に三回、プールに行きます. With 週, 月 and 年, the 一 is often dropped: 週に二回, 月に一回, 年に一度.

formation.form: Period (一日, 一週間, 一か月, 一年; or 週, 月, 年) + に + number + 回／度
formation.note: 回 is the everyday counter for times; 度 is a little more formal.

examples.japanese: 一週間に三回、プールで泳ぎます。
examples.reading: いっしゅうかんにさんかい、プールでおよぎます。
examples.romaji: isshūkan ni sankai, pūru de oyogimasu.
examples.english: I swim at the pool three times a week.

examples.japanese: この薬は一日に二回飲んでください。
examples.reading: このくすりはいちにちににかいのんでください。
examples.romaji: kono kusuri wa ichinichi ni nikai nonde kudasai.
examples.english: Please take this medicine twice a day.

examples.japanese: 母には月に一度電話します。
examples.reading: ははにはつきにいちどでんわします。
examples.romaji: haha ni wa tsuki ni ichido denwa shimasu.
examples.english: I call my mother once a month.

mistake.wrong: 三回一週間にジムに行きます。
mistake.problem: This follows the English order, "three times a week". In Japanese the period comes first and frames the count.
mistake.right: 一週間に三回ジムに行きます。

review.note: Is 一週間で三回 worth mentioning as a neighbour (a total within one week, rather than a regular rate)? Left out as uncertain.

entries.title: Wanting a thing
entries.meaning: N がほしい: "I want N". ほしい is an い-adjective for wanting a thing, said of yourself, or asked of the listener.
entries.when: Use it to say what you want to have: 新しいかばんがほしいです. In a question, ask what the listener wants: 何がほしいですか. For what someone else wants, see ～たがる.
entries.why: ほしい is an い-adjective describing a feeling: the thing is "wanted" by you. Like other feeling words such as 好き or 痛い, it reports an inner state that only the person feeling it can know, so in a plain statement the one who wants is the speaker, and in a question, the listener. The wanted thing is marked with が, not を, because ほしい is an adjective, not a verb: the thing is what the feeling is about, just as in 犬が好き. ほしい is for things; to want to do something, use the verb with たい.

formation.note: Polite: ほしいです. Negative: ほしくない; past: ほしかった. は replaces が for contrast: お金はほしくないです.

examples.japanese: 新しいパソコンがほしいです。
examples.reading: あたらしいパソコンがほしいです。
examples.romaji: atarashii pasokon ga hoshii desu.
examples.english: I want a new computer.

examples.japanese: 誕生日に何がほしいですか。
examples.reading: たんじょうびになにがほしいですか。
examples.romaji: tanjōbi ni nani ga hoshii desu ka.
examples.english: What do you want for your birthday?

examples.japanese: 子どものころ、犬がとてもほしかったです。
examples.reading: こどものころ、いぬがとてもほしかったです。
examples.romaji: kodomo no koro, inu ga totemo hoshikatta desu.
examples.english: When I was a child, I really wanted a dog.

mistake.wrong: 水をほしいです。
mistake.problem: ほしい is an adjective, not a verb, so the thing wanted is not its object. It takes が.
mistake.right: 水がほしいです。

distinguish_from.note: たい is for wanting to do something (水を飲みたい). ほしい is for wanting a thing (水がほしい).
てほしい is for wanting someone else to do something (手伝ってほしい). ほしい on its own wants a thing.
ほしい states your own want. For another person, ほしがる reports the want as it shows.

entries.title: Someone else wants to (as it shows)
entries.meaning: V-たがる: a third person shows signs of wanting to do V; "X wants to V", judged from how they act.
entries.when: Use it to say what someone other than you wants to do, going by what they say or do: 弟は外で遊びたがっています. It is usually in the ている form for a current want, or the plain form for a habit. ほしがる does the same for wanting a thing.
entries.why: たい and ほしい are feelings only the person feeling them can know, so Japanese avoids stating another person's want as plain fact. がる turns an inner feeling into outward behaviour: "show signs of wanting". So 行きたがる reports what can be seen from outside. It makes an ordinary godan verb, and since it now describes an action, the object takes を: 水を飲みたがる, ゲームをほしがる. For the same reason it is not used of yourself in an ordinary statement.

formation.note: 行きたがる, 行きたがっている, 行きたがらない. Polite: 行きたがっています.
The same change made from ほしい.

examples.japanese: 弟は毎日外で遊びたがります。
examples.reading: おとうとはまいにちそとであそびたがります。
examples.romaji: otōto wa mainichi soto de asobitagarimasu.
examples.english: My little brother wants to play outside every day.

examples.japanese: 息子が新しいゲームをほしがっています。
examples.reading: むすこがあたらしいゲームをほしがっています。
examples.romaji: musuko ga atarashii gēmu o hoshigatte imasu.
examples.english: My son wants a new video game.

examples.japanese: 子どもは野菜を食べたがりません。
examples.reading: こどもはやさいをたべたがりません。
examples.romaji: kodomo wa yasai o tabetagarimasen.
examples.english: The children don't want to eat vegetables.

mistake.wrong: 友だちは日本へ行きたいです。
mistake.problem: A plain statement with たい reports the want as if from inside. About someone else, say what shows (行きたがっています) or report what they said (行きたいと言っています).
mistake.right: 友だちは日本へ行きたがっています。

distinguish_from.note: たい states your own want, or asks the listener's. たがる reports someone else's want as it shows.

review.note: Should the entry warn that たがる can sound presumptuous or childish when said of someone of higher status? Left out as unsure how strong that is.

entries.title: Maybe, might
entries.meaning: Plain form + かもしれない: "may", "might"; the speaker thinks it possible but is far from sure.
entries.when: Use it for a possibility you cannot rule out: 午後から雨が降るかもしれません, "it might rain this afternoon". It works for the past and present too: かぎを忘れたかもしれない. Polite: かもしれません. Casual speech often shortens it to かも.
entries.why: The pieces say it: か is "whether", も is "even", しれない is "cannot be known". "Whether it is so cannot even be known": the speaker admits a possibility without committing to it. Because it only says the thing is possible, the chance can be quite low, lower than with でしょう, which leans towards yes. A noun or な-adjective goes straight before か with no だ, just as it does in a plain question (学生か).

formation.form: Verb / い-adjective (plain form) + かもしれない
formation.note: 降るかもしれない, 降ったかもしれない, 降らないかもしれない; 高いかもしれない.

formation.form: Noun / な-adjective + かもしれない
formation.note: No だ: 雨かもしれない, 静かかもしれない.

examples.japanese: 午後から雨が降るかもしれません。
examples.reading: ごごからあめがふるかもしれません。
examples.romaji: gogo kara ame ga furu kamo shiremasen.
examples.english: It might rain from the afternoon.

examples.japanese: かぎを家に忘れたかもしれない。
examples.reading: かぎをいえにわすれたかもしれない。
examples.romaji: kagi o ie ni wasureta kamo shirenai.
examples.english: I might have left my keys at home.

examples.japanese: あの人は先生かもしれません。
examples.reading: あのひとはせんせいかもしれません。
examples.romaji: ano hito wa sensei kamo shiremasen.
examples.english: That person might be a teacher.

mistake.wrong: あの人は学生だかもしれません。
mistake.problem: かもしれない follows a noun or な-adjective directly. The だ is dropped.
mistake.right: あの人は学生かもしれません。

distinguish_from.note: でしょう says "probably": the speaker leans towards yes. かもしれない says "maybe": only that it is possible.

entries.title: Suggesting, "why don't you…?"
entries.meaning: V-たらどうですか: "how about V-ing?"; a suggestion about what the listener could do.
entries.when: Use it to suggest a course of action to someone, often about a problem they have: 疲れているなら、少し休んだらどうですか. More politely, たらいかがですか; casually, たらどう？
entries.why: たら sets up a condition, "if you did V", and どうですか asks "how would that be?". So the sentence asks the listener to picture doing V and judge it, and leaves the decision with them. It is a suggestion for the listener alone: it is not an invitation to do something together, which is ませんか or ましょう. Because it tells the listener what they could do, it is advice, and some care is needed in using it to people above you.

formation.form: V (た-form) + ら + どうですか
formation.note: 休んだらどうですか. Politer: たらいかがですか. Casual: たらどう？

examples.japanese: 疲れているなら、少し休んだらどうですか。
examples.reading: つかれているなら、すこしやすんだらどうですか。
examples.romaji: tsukarete iru nara, sukoshi yasundara dō desu ka.
examples.english: If you're tired, why don't you rest a little?

examples.japanese: わからないなら、先生に聞いたらどうですか。
examples.reading: わからないなら、せんせいにきいたらどうですか。
examples.romaji: wakaranai nara, sensei ni kiitara dō desu ka.
examples.english: If you don't understand, why not ask the teacher?

examples.japanese: そんなに好きなら、買ったらどう？
examples.reading: そんなにすきなら、かったらどう？
examples.romaji: sonna ni suki nara, kattara dō?
examples.english: If you like it that much, why not buy it?

mistake.wrong: いっしょに映画を見たらどうですか。
mistake.problem: たらどうですか suggests something for the listener to do. With いっしょに you are inviting them to do it with you, which is ませんか.
mistake.right: いっしょに映画を見ませんか。

distinguish_from.note: ほうがいい says one choice is better and sounds firmer. たらどうですか offers an idea and leaves the choice to the listener.
ませんか invites the listener to do something with you. たらどうですか suggests something for the listener alone.

review.note: How presumptuous is たらどうですか (and たらいかがですか) towards a superior? The entry only says some care is needed.

entries.title: As many as (more than expected)
entries.meaning: Number + も: stresses that an amount is large, "as many as", "a whole…"; 一 + counter + も + negative is "not even one".
entries.when: Use it after a number and counter when the amount strikes you as a lot: 一時間も待ちました, "I waited a whole hour". With 一 and a negative verb it means "not a single one": 一人もいません.
entries.why: も means "too, even". After a quantity it says "even this much": the speaker measures the amount against what was expected and finds it more. So it carries surprise or complaint; 一時間待ちました only states the time. With a negative, "not even one" becomes "none at all": 一つもない. A number with its counter normally sits just before the verb without a particle, and も simply follows it there.

formation.note: 三時間も, 五つも, 二杯も.

formation.form: 一 + counter + も + negative verb
formation.note: 一人もいない, 一回も行ったことがない.

examples.japanese: 駅で一時間も待ちました。
examples.reading: えきでいちじかんもまちました。
examples.romaji: eki de ichijikan mo machimashita.
examples.english: I waited a whole hour at the station.

examples.japanese: 兄はケーキを五つも食べました。
examples.reading: あにはケーキをいつつもたべました。
examples.romaji: ani wa kēki o itsutsu mo tabemashita.
examples.english: My older brother ate as many as five pieces of cake.

examples.japanese: 教室には学生が一人もいません。
examples.reading: きょうしつにはがくせいがひとりもいません。
examples.romaji: kyōshitsu ni wa gakusei ga hitori mo imasen.
examples.english: There isn't a single student in the classroom.

mistake.wrong: 今朝、りんごを一つも食べました。
mistake.problem: 一 + counter + も means "not even one" and needs a negative verb. To say you ate one, leave out も.
mistake.right: 今朝、りんごを一つ食べました。

distinguish_from.note: After a noun, も means "too, also" (私も). After a number and counter, it means "as many as".

entries.title: Only (and not enough)
entries.meaning: X しか + negative: "only X", "nothing but X"; stresses that X is little, or less than wanted.
entries.when: Use it to say something is limited to X, usually with a feeling that it is not enough: 五百円しかありません, "I only have 500 yen". It follows nouns and numbers, and can follow other particles: 日曜日にしか, 田中さんとしか.
entries.why: しか marks X as the one exception to a negative: "apart from X, there is none". So the verb must be negative, even though English says it positively ("I only have…"). Built as "nothing except X", it stresses shortage: 五百円しかない sounds like "just 500 yen, not enough", where 五百円だけある is neutral. しか replaces が and を; other particles stay in front of it (にしか, からしか).

formation.note: しかない, しかありません, しか食べない. が and を are dropped.
にしか, でしか, としか, からしか.

examples.japanese: 財布に五百円しかありません。
examples.reading: さいふにごひゃくえんしかありません。
examples.romaji: saifu ni gohyakuen shika arimasen.
examples.english: I only have 500 yen in my wallet.

examples.japanese: 朝はコーヒーしか飲みません。
examples.reading: あさはコーヒーしかのみません。
examples.romaji: asa wa kōhī shika nomimasen.
examples.english: In the morning, I drink nothing but coffee.

examples.japanese: この店は日曜日にしか開いていません。
examples.reading: このみせはにちようびにしかあいていません。
examples.romaji: kono mise wa nichiyōbi ni shika aite imasen.
examples.english: This shop is only open on Sundays.

mistake.wrong: 五百円しかあります。
mistake.problem: しか needs a negative verb, even though English says "only have".
mistake.right: 五百円しかありません。

distinguish_from.note: だけ is neutral and goes with a positive verb (五百円だけある). しか needs a negative and stresses that it is not much.

entries.title: Do something in advance, or leave it as it is
entries.meaning: V-ておく: do V now, ready for later; or do V and leave the result as it is.
entries.when: Use it for preparation (旅行の前にホテルを予約しておく), for getting something done ahead of time, and for leaving a state as it is on purpose (窓を開けておいてください, "please leave the window open"). Casual speech shortens ておく to とく, and でおく to どく: 買っとく, 読んどく.
entries.why: おく means "put, place". After the て-form it says "do V and put it in place": the action is done now with a later need in mind. That is why it covers both preparing and leaving something as it is for a reason. The sentence is about what the person does, so the object keeps を, unlike てある, which describes the state a thing is left in and usually marks the thing with が.

formation.note: Polite: ておきます. Request: ておいてください. Casual: とく／どく (買っとく, 読んどく).

examples.japanese: 旅行の前に、ホテルを予約しておきました。
examples.reading: りょこうのまえに、ホテルをよやくしておきました。
examples.romaji: ryokō no mae ni, hoteru o yoyaku shite okimashita.
examples.english: I booked a hotel before the trip.

examples.japanese: 友だちが来るから、ビールを買っておきます。
examples.reading: ともだちがくるから、ビールをかっておきます。
examples.romaji: tomodachi ga kuru kara, bīru o katte okimasu.
examples.english: Friends are coming over, so I'll buy some beer.

examples.japanese: 暑いので、窓を開けておいてください。
examples.reading: あついので、まどをあけておいてください。
examples.romaji: atsui node, mado o akete oite kudasai.
examples.english: It's hot, so please leave the window open.

mistake.wrong: 窓が開けておきます。
mistake.problem: ておく says what someone does, so the thing acted on is the object and takes を. が with a transitive verb here is borrowed from てある, which describes the resulting state.
mistake.right: 窓を開けておきます。

distinguish_from.note: ておく says what someone does now for later (窓を開けておく). てある describes the state that has been prepared (窓が開けてある).

entries.title: Let's…, I'll… (the volitional form)
entries.meaning: The volitional form (食べよう, 行こう): "let's V" in casual speech, or the speaker's own will, "I'll V".
entries.when: Use it in casual speech to suggest doing something together (映画を見よう, "let's watch a film") or to state, to yourself or others, what you have decided to do (もう寝よう, "I'll go to bed now"). With か it offers or consults: 持とうか, "shall I carry it?". It is the plain counterpart of ましょう, and the base of ～ようと思う.
entries.why: The volitional form expresses the speaker's will. Whether it comes out as "let's" or "I'll" depends on who is included: about something you and the listener can do together, it invites; about yourself, it declares an intention. Ichidan verbs add よう to the stem (食べよう, 見よう). Godan verbs move their last sound to the お-row and add う (行く → 行こう, 飲む → 飲もう, 待つ → 待とう, 買う → 買おう), which is why lists name the form by both endings, ～よう and ～おう. Because it states a will, everyday speech does not use it for things nobody controls, such as the weather.

formation.note: 食べる → 食べよう, 起きる → 起きよう, 見る → 見よう.

formation.form: Godan verb (last sound to the お-row) + う
formation.note: 行く → 行こう, 飲む → 飲もう, 話す → 話そう, 待つ → 待とう, 帰る → 帰ろう, 買う → 買おう.

formation.form: する → しよう; 来る → 来よう (こよう)

formation.note: Offers or consults: 持とうか, "shall I carry it?"; どうしようか, "what shall we do?". Polite: ましょうか.

examples.japanese: 疲れたね。ちょっと休もう。
examples.reading: つかれたね。ちょっとやすもう。
examples.romaji: tsukareta ne. chotto yasumō.
examples.english: We're tired, aren't we. Let's take a short break.

examples.japanese: 明日から毎日走ろう。
examples.reading: あしたからまいにちはしろう。
examples.romaji: ashita kara mainichi hashirō.
examples.english: From tomorrow, I'll run every day.
examples.note: Said to yourself, it states an intention.

examples.japanese: 重そうだね。持とうか。
examples.reading: おもそうだね。もとうか。
examples.romaji: omosō da ne. motō ka.
examples.english: That looks heavy. Shall I carry it?

examples.japanese: 週末、いっしょに映画を見よう。
examples.reading: しゅうまつ、いっしょにえいがをみよう。
examples.romaji: shūmatsu, issho ni eiga o miyō.
examples.english: Let's watch a film together this weekend.

mistake.wrong: 早く行きよう。
mistake.problem: 行く is a godan verb, so よう is not added to its stem. Its last sound moves to the お-row and takes う.
mistake.right: 早く行こう。

distinguish_from.note: ましょう is the polite form of the same will and invitation. The volitional form is the plain one, for friends and family and for talking to yourself.
ようと思う reports an intention you hold ("I'm thinking of…"). The volitional form on its own states the decision, or invites.

review.note: Tanos lists ～よう (497) and ～おう (498) separately. They are one form, the volitional, split by verb class, so this entry covers both; OJG-0054 is left as a stub for the owner to retire as a duplicate.

entries.title: Doing something for someone
entries.meaning: V-てあげる: do V for someone else's benefit; the favour goes out from you or your side.
entries.when: Use it when you, or someone on your side, do something for another person: 妹に本を読んであげました, "I read a book to my little sister". The person who benefits keeps whatever particle the verb needs (友だちを駅まで送ってあげた, 友だちの宿題を見てあげた), or takes に where the verb has no place for them.
entries.why: あげる is "give", outward from the speaker's side. After the て-form it gives the action itself as a favour, so the direction is the same: from me, or my side, to others. Because it presents what you do as a kindness, saying it to the person you are helping can sound condescending, like "I'll do you the favour". Offers are made with ましょうか instead (持ちましょうか). For a favour that comes to you, use てくれる or てもらう.

formation.note: Polite: てあげます. Humble, towards someone above the receiver: てさしあげる (OJG-0326), which has the same problem when said to their face.

examples.japanese: 妹に本を読んであげました。
examples.reading: いもうとにほんをよんであげました。
examples.romaji: imōto ni hon o yonde agemashita.
examples.english: I read a book to my little sister.

examples.japanese: 友だちを車で駅まで送ってあげました。
examples.reading: ともだちをくるまでえきまでおくってあげました。
examples.romaji: tomodachi o kuruma de eki made okutte agemashita.
examples.english: I gave my friend a lift to the station.

examples.japanese: 兄は友だちに料理を作ってあげました。
examples.reading: あにはともだちにりょうりをつくってあげました。
examples.romaji: ani wa tomodachi ni ryōri o tsukutte agemashita.
examples.english: My older brother cooked for his friend.

mistake.wrong: 先生、荷物を持ってあげます。
mistake.problem: てあげる frames your help as a favour you are granting. Said to the person you are helping, and especially to a superior, it sounds condescending. Offer with ましょうか.
mistake.right: 先生、荷物を持ちましょうか。

distinguish_from.note: てくれる is a favour that comes in, to you or your side. てあげる is a favour going out from your side.
あげる gives a thing. てあげる gives an action.

entries.title: Someone does something for me
entries.meaning: V-てくれる: someone does V for the speaker or the speaker's side; the doer is the subject, and the favour comes in.
entries.when: Use it when someone does something that benefits you or someone on your side, and you want to show it was a kindness: 友だちが駅まで迎えに来てくれました. The doer is the subject (が or は); since the favour comes to you, 私に is usually left out. It also makes casual requests: 手伝ってくれる？
entries.why: くれる is "give (to me)": it points only inward, towards the speaker's side. After the て-form it hands an action to you as a gift. 母が弁当を作りました only states a fact; 母が弁当を作ってくれました shows it was done for you and that you appreciate it, and leaving it out where someone did you a favour can sound cold. Because the direction is fixed, the one who benefits is always you or your side, never an outsider.

formation.note: Polite: てくれます. Honorific: てくださる (OJG-0326). Requests: てくれる？, てくれませんか (OJG-0327).

examples.japanese: 友だちが駅まで迎えに来てくれました。
examples.reading: ともだちがえきまでむかえにきてくれました。
examples.romaji: tomodachi ga eki made mukae ni kite kuremashita.
examples.english: My friend came to meet me at the station.

examples.japanese: 母がお弁当を作ってくれました。
examples.reading: ははがおべんとうをつくってくれました。
examples.romaji: haha ga obentō o tsukutte kuremashita.
examples.english: My mother made me a packed lunch.

examples.japanese: 田中さんが道を教えてくれました。
examples.reading: たなかさんがみちをおしえてくれました。
examples.romaji: tanaka-san ga michi o oshiete kuremashita.
examples.english: Tanaka-san showed me the way.

mistake.wrong: 私は友だちに宿題を手伝ってくれました。
mistake.problem: With てくれる the doer is the subject and the favour comes to you. 私は makes you the doer. Make the friend the subject, or keep 私は and use てもらう.
mistake.right: 友だちが宿題を手伝ってくれました。

distinguish_from.note: Same event, other viewpoint. てくれる makes the doer the subject; てもらう makes the receiver the subject and marks the doer with に.
てあげる is a favour going out from your side. てくれる is one coming in.

entries.title: Having someone do something for you
entries.meaning: V-てもらう: have someone do V for you; the receiver is the subject, and the doer is marked with に.
entries.when: Use it to tell a favour from the receiver's side: 友だちに宿題を手伝ってもらいました, "I had my friend help me with my homework". It also covers getting something done by someone (時計を直してもらう, "get a watch repaired") and forms polite requests (てもらえませんか).
entries.why: もらう is "receive". After the て-form it receives an action: you receive someone's doing V. So the subject is the one who benefits, and the one who acts is the source, marked with に just as in 友だちにもらった. Compared with てくれる, the event is the same but told from the receiver's side, and it can suggest you asked for it or arranged it. For a kindness nobody asked for, てくれる is often more natural.

formation.form: (receiver は) doer に … V (て-form) + もらう
formation.note: Polite: てもらいます. Humble: ていただく (OJG-0326). Request: てもらえませんか (OJG-0327).

examples.japanese: 友だちに宿題を手伝ってもらいました。
examples.reading: ともだちにしゅくだいをてつだってもらいました。
examples.romaji: tomodachi ni shukudai o tetsudatte moraimashita.
examples.english: I had my friend help me with my homework.

examples.japanese: 店の人に写真を撮ってもらいました。
examples.reading: みせのひとにしゃしんをとってもらいました。
examples.romaji: mise no hito ni shashin o totte moraimashita.
examples.english: I had someone from the shop take a photo for me.

examples.japanese: 壊れた時計を直してもらいました。
examples.reading: こわれたとけいをなおしてもらいました。
examples.romaji: kowareta tokei o naoshite moraimashita.
examples.english: I had my broken watch repaired.

mistake.wrong: 友だちが私に本を貸してもらいました。
mistake.problem: With てもらう the subject is the receiver. Here the friend did the lending, so either make yourself the subject and mark the friend with に, or keep the friend as subject with てくれる.
mistake.right: 私は友だちに本を貸してもらいました。

distinguish_from.note: てくれる tells the same favour with the doer as subject. てもらう tells it with the receiver as subject.
もらう receives a thing. てもらう receives an action.

entries.title: Could you possibly…? (a very polite request)
entries.meaning: V-ていただけませんか: "could you please V?"; a very polite request, asked as whether you may receive the favour.
entries.when: Use it for polite requests to strangers, customers, teachers, or anyone above you, especially for a real favour: もう少しゆっくり話していただけませんか. Less formal members of the same family are てもらえませんか, てくださいませんか and てくれませんか.
entries.why: いただく is the humble verb for "receive", and いただける is its potential form, "can receive". ませんか asks in the negative. Put together: "can't I receive your doing V?". The request is softened twice: it asks about your receiving instead of telling the listener to act, and the negative question leaves room for no. Since the speaker is the one receiving, the listener, who does the action, is usually not named.

formation.form: V (て-form) + いただけませんか
formation.note: いただけますか is a little less soft. いただけないでしょうか is softer still.

examples.japanese: もう少しゆっくり話していただけませんか。
examples.reading: もうすこしゆっくりはなしていただけませんか。
examples.romaji: mō sukoshi yukkuri hanashite itadakemasen ka.
examples.english: Could you speak a little more slowly, please?

examples.japanese: すみません、この字の読み方を教えていただけませんか。
examples.reading: すみません、このじのよみかたをおしえていただけませんか。
examples.romaji: sumimasen, kono ji no yomikata o oshiete itadakemasen ka.
examples.english: Excuse me, could you tell me how to read this character?

examples.japanese: 明日までに書類を送っていただけませんか。
examples.reading: あしたまでにしょるいをおくっていただけませんか。
examples.romaji: ashita made ni shorui o okutte itadakemasen ka.
examples.english: Could you send the documents by tomorrow?

mistake.wrong: 先生、この本を貸していただきませんか。
mistake.problem: The request needs the potential form いただける, "can I receive". いただきませんか asks "won't (we) receive?", which is not a request to the listener.
mistake.right: 先生、この本を貸していただけませんか。

distinguish_from.note: てくれませんか, てもらえませんか and てくださいませんか make the same request less formally. ていただけませんか is the most polite of the everyday forms.

review.note: Overlaps OJG-0327 (the other request forms) and OJG-0326 (ていただく); a candidate to merge into one entry for the request family.

entries.title: I hope…, it would be good if…
entries.meaning: Plain form + といいです(ね): "I hope…", "it would be nice if…"; a wish for something you cannot bring about yourself.
entries.when: Use it to hope for an outcome that is not in your hands: 明日晴れるといいですね, "I hope it's sunny tomorrow". With ね, it shares the hope with the listener, often as a kind wish for them: 早くよくなるといいですね. For your own hopes, といいんですが or, casually, といいなあ is common.
entries.why: This と is the conditional "if A, then B", so といい says "if A happens, it's good". Saying an outcome would be good is how Japanese states a hope without claiming control over it. When the hope is about the future, the part before と is in the non-past (晴れる), because the outcome still lies ahead. A trailing が or けど (といいんですが) adds "but I can't be sure", which suits your own hopes.

formation.form: Verb / い-adjective (plain form) + といいです(ね)
formation.note: 晴れるといい, 安いといい; negative 雨が降らないといい.

formation.form: Noun / な-adjective + だ + といい
formation.note: 晴れだといい, 元気だといい.

formation.form: … といいんですが／といいなあ
formation.note: For your own hopes, or to add that you are unsure.

examples.japanese: 明日、晴れるといいですね。
examples.reading: あした、はれるといいですね。
examples.romaji: ashita, hareru to ii desu ne.
examples.english: I hope it's sunny tomorrow.

examples.japanese: お母さんの病気が早くよくなるといいですね。
examples.reading: おかあさんのびょうきがはやくよくなるといいですね。
examples.romaji: okāsan no byōki ga hayaku yoku naru to ii desu ne.
examples.english: I hope your mother gets better soon.

examples.japanese: 試験に合格できるといいんですが。
examples.reading: しけんにごうかくできるといいんですが。
examples.romaji: shiken ni gōkaku dekiru to ii n desu ga.
examples.english: I hope I can pass the exam.

mistake.wrong: 明日、晴れたといいですね。
mistake.problem: The hope is about tomorrow, so the part before と stays non-past. The た-form belongs with たら (晴れたらいいですね), a different pattern with a similar meaning.
mistake.right: 明日、晴れるといいですね。

distinguish_from.note: たらいい and ばいい can also express a hope (晴れたらいい), but they are mainly for asking and giving advice (どうしたらいいですか). といい is mainly a wish.

review.note: A た-form before といい can hope about something already decided (間に合ったといいんですが, "I hope he made it"); the entry leaves this out for N4. Is that the right call?

entries.title: Sorry for doing…
entries.meaning: V-てすみません: "sorry for V-ing"; apologises for a specific thing you did or failed to do.
entries.when: Use it to name what you are apologising for: 遅れてすみません, "sorry I'm late". For something you did not do, use the negative て-form なくて: 返事をしなくてすみません. For something over and done, すみませんでした; more formally, て申し訳ありません.
entries.why: The て-form here gives a cause: "I did V, and so, I'm sorry". The part before すみません names what the apology is for. When the cause is something you failed to do, the negative て-form that gives a reason is なくて. ないで means "without doing" or asks someone not to do something; it does not give a cause, so it does not fit here.

formation.note: Past, for something finished: てすみませんでした.

formation.form: V (negative) → なくて + すみません
formation.note: 来なくて, 連絡しなくて.

formation.form: V (て-form) + 申し訳ありません
formation.note: More formal, for customers and superiors.

examples.japanese: 遅れてすみません。
examples.reading: おくれてすみません。
examples.romaji: okurete sumimasen.
examples.english: Sorry I'm late.

examples.japanese: 昨日は電話に出なくてすみませんでした。
examples.reading: きのうはでんわにでなくてすみませんでした。
examples.romaji: kinō wa denwa ni denakute sumimasen deshita.
examples.english: Sorry I didn't answer the phone yesterday.

examples.japanese: 夜遅くに電話してすみません。
examples.reading: よるおそくにでんわしてすみません。
examples.romaji: yoru osoku ni denwa shite sumimasen.
examples.english: Sorry for calling so late at night.

mistake.wrong: 返事をしないですみません。
mistake.problem: The part before すみません gives the reason for the apology, and a negative reason takes なくて. ないで means "without doing" and does not give a reason.
mistake.right: 返事をしなくてすみません。

entries.title: Looks like, looks about to
entries.meaning: Stem + そうです: "looks (adjective)", judged from appearance; after a verb stem, "looks as if it's about to V".
entries.when: Use it for your impression of something in front of you: このケーキはおいしそうです, "this cake looks delicious". After a verb stem, it says something looks about to happen: 雨が降りそうです, "it looks like it's going to rain". Before a noun it becomes そうな (おいしそうなケーキ), and before a verb, そうに (楽しそうに遊ぶ).
entries.why: This そう gives your own judgement from what you can see or sense, before you know for sure: the cake looks good, but you have not tasted it yet. That is why adjectives that simply name what you see, such as 赤い or きれい, are usually said directly instead. It joins to a stem, not to a full form: い-adjectives drop い (高い → 高そう), な-adjectives use the stem (元気そう), and verbs use the ます-stem (降りそう). The full form before そう (高いそう) is a different point, the hearsay そう. Two irregulars: いい → よさそう, ない → なさそう.

formation.note: 高そう, おいしそう. いい → よさそう; ない → なさそう (おいしくなさそう).
元気そう, ひまそう.
降りそう, 落ちそう.

formation.form: そうだ／そうです; そうな + noun; そうに + verb

examples.japanese: このケーキはおいしそうですね。
examples.reading: このケーキはおいしそうですね。
examples.romaji: kono kēki wa oishisō desu ne.
examples.english: This cake looks delicious.

examples.japanese: 空が暗いです。雨が降りそうです。
examples.reading: そらがくらいです。あめがふりそうです。
examples.romaji: sora ga kurai desu. ame ga furisō desu.
examples.english: The sky is dark. It looks like it's going to rain.

examples.japanese: 子どもたちが楽しそうに遊んでいます。
examples.reading: こどもたちがたのしそうにあそんでいます。
examples.romaji: kodomotachi ga tanoshisō ni asonde imasu.
examples.english: The children are playing, looking like they're having fun.

examples.japanese: 棚の上のコップが落ちそうです。
examples.reading: たなのうえのコップがおちそうです。
examples.romaji: tana no ue no koppu ga ochisō desu.
examples.english: The glass on the shelf looks like it's about to fall.

mistake.wrong: このかばんは高いそうです。
mistake.problem: Meant as "looks expensive", but with the full 高い this is the hearsay そう, "I hear it's expensive". For how it looks, drop the い.
mistake.right: このかばんは高そうです。

distinguish_from.note: The hearsay そう follows a full plain form (高いそう, 降るそう) and reports what you heard. This そう follows a stem (高そう, 降りそう) and gives your impression.
ようだ is a judgement from evidence of any kind, often after the fact. そう after a stem is an impression from appearance, and with verbs, a sense that something is about to happen.

review.note: Is the restriction on visual adjectives (赤そう, きれいそう usually avoided for what is plainly in view) stated at the right strength?

entries.title: Making or letting someone do something (the causative)
entries.meaning: Causative V-させる／V-せる: make someone do V, or let them; the one who causes it is the subject.
entries.when: Use it when one person makes or allows another to act: 母は弟に野菜を食べさせました, "my mother made my brother eat vegetables"; 子どもを公園で遊ばせました, "I let the children play in the park". Whether it means "make" or "let" comes from the context. Asking permission with させてください is its own point (OJG-0346).
entries.why: The causative adds a causer on top of an action: the causer becomes the subject, and the one who actually acts is moved to another particle. With a verb that already has a を-object, the one who acts takes に (弟に野菜を食べさせる), since a clause does not normally carry two を. With a verb that has no object, it can take を or に; を tends to mean the person had no choice, and に that they were allowed to do what they wanted. The causative verb is itself an ichidan verb (食べさせます, 食べさせた).

formation.note: 行く → 行かせる, 読む → 読ませる, 遊ぶ → 遊ばせる, 買う → 買わせる.
食べる → 食べさせる, 見る → 見させる.

formation.form: する → させる; 来る → 来させる (こさせる)

examples.japanese: 母は弟に野菜を食べさせました。
examples.reading: はははおとうとにやさいをたべさせました。
examples.romaji: haha wa otōto ni yasai o tabesasemashita.
examples.english: My mother made my little brother eat vegetables.

examples.japanese: 先生は学生に作文を書かせました。
examples.reading: せんせいはがくせいにさくぶんをかかせました。
examples.romaji: sensei wa gakusei ni sakubun o kakasemashita.
examples.english: The teacher had the students write an essay.

examples.japanese: 子どもを公園で遊ばせました。
examples.reading: こどもをこうえんであそばせました。
examples.romaji: kodomo o kōen de asobasemashita.
examples.english: I let the children play in the park.

mistake.wrong: 母は弟を野菜を食べさせました。
mistake.problem: 食べる already has a を-object (野菜), and a clause normally carries only one を, so the one made to eat takes に.
mistake.right: 母は弟に野菜を食べさせました。

distinguish_from.note: させられる is the causative made passive, told from the side of the one made to act. させる is told from the causer's side.
させてください uses the causative to ask to be allowed to do something yourself.

entries.title: Do it! (a firm instruction from above)
entries.meaning: V (ます-stem) + なさい: a firm but not rough instruction, used by parents, teachers and in test questions.
entries.when: Use it when someone with authority tells someone else to do something: a parent to a child (早く寝なさい), a teacher to pupils, and in written instructions on tests and exercises (正しいものを選びなさい). Adults do not use it to other adults as equals, or to anyone above them.
entries.why: なさい comes from なさる, the honorific verb for "do", so it sounds gentler than the plain command form (寝ろ, 食べろ). It is still a command, and using it puts the speaker in the position of someone entitled to give orders, which is why it belongs to parents, teachers and written instructions. Like ます, it joins to the ます-stem. It has no negative form; to tell someone not to do something, other forms are used (～てはいけません, ～ないで).

formation.note: 寝る → 寝なさい, 食べる → 食べなさい, 勉強する → 勉強しなさい, 来る → 来なさい.

examples.japanese: 早く寝なさい。
examples.reading: はやくねなさい。
examples.romaji: hayaku nenasai.
examples.english: Go to bed now.

examples.japanese: 野菜も食べなさい。
examples.reading: やさいもたべなさい。
examples.romaji: yasai mo tabenasai.
examples.english: Eat your vegetables too.

examples.japanese: 正しいものを一つ選びなさい。
examples.reading: ただしいものをひとつえらびなさい。
examples.romaji: tadashii mono o hitotsu erabinasai.
examples.english: Choose the one correct answer.
examples.note: A typical test instruction.

mistake.wrong: 田中さん、この書類を見なさい。
mistake.problem: Said to a colleague. なさい is an instruction from above, and between adults at work it is rude. Ask with てください, or more politely with ていただけませんか.
mistake.right: 田中さん、この書類を見てください。

entries.title: If (the condition for a result)
entries.meaning: The ば-form: "if A, (then) B"; A is the condition that brings about or allows B.
entries.when: Use it for a condition and what follows from it: 安ければ買います, "if it's cheap, I'll buy it"; このボタンを押せば開きます, "if you press this button, it opens". It suits general truths, hypotheses, and questions about how to get a result: どうすれば, "what do I have to do to…". For advice, see ばいい (OJG-0348).
entries.why: The ば-form puts the weight on the condition: B holds as long as A is met. That makes it sound a little more logical and neutral than たら. It also explains a restriction: when A is an action and B is a request, an order, an invitation or the speaker's own intention, ば usually sounds unnatural, because B is meant to follow A in time, which is what たら says. When A is a state (ある, いる, adjectives, できる), ば is fine even before a request: 時間があれば、手伝ってください.

formation.form: Godan verb (last sound to the え-row) + ば
formation.note: 行く → 行けば, 飲む → 飲めば, 買う → 買えば, ある → あれば.
食べる → 食べれば, 見る → 見れば.

formation.form: する → すれば; 来る → 来れば (くれば)

formation.note: 高い → 高ければ; いい → よければ; ない → なければ.

formation.form: Noun / な-adjective + なら (or であれば)
formation.note: The ば-form of だ is なら; であれば is more formal.

examples.japanese: 安ければ、買います。
examples.reading: やすければ、かいます。
examples.romaji: yasukereba, kaimasu.
examples.english: If it's cheap, I'll buy it.

examples.japanese: このボタンを押せば、ドアが開きます。
examples.reading: このボタンをおせば、ドアがあきます。
examples.romaji: kono botan o oseba, doa ga akimasu.
examples.english: If you press this button, the door opens.

examples.japanese: 時間があれば、手伝ってください。
examples.reading: じかんがあれば、てつだってください。
examples.romaji: jikan ga areba, tetsudatte kudasai.
examples.english: If you have time, please help me.
examples.note: A is a state (ある), so a request after ば is fine.

examples.japanese: 急げば、間に合いますよ。
examples.reading: いそげば、まにあいますよ。
examples.romaji: isogeba, maniaimasu yo.
examples.english: If you hurry, you'll make it.

mistake.wrong: 家に帰れば、電話してください。
mistake.problem: The first part is an action and the second is a request meant to follow it. ば usually sounds unnatural here; たら says "once A has happened, B".
mistake.right: 家に帰ったら、電話してください。

distinguish_from.note: たら says B follows once A has happened, and works with requests and intentions. ば focuses on A as the condition, and avoids requests after an action.
と is for results that always or automatically follow. ば covers those and also one-off hypotheses.
なら takes up something given and comments on it, in any order in time.

review.note: The restriction on ば before requests and intentions is stated as "usually sounds unnatural"; is that the right strength for N4?

entries.title: Even if, even though
entries.meaning: て-form + も: "even if", "even though"; B holds whatever happens with A.
entries.when: Use it to say B happens or holds regardless of A: 雨が降っても行きます, "even if it rains, I'll go". It works for hypotheses and for facts: 何回聞いても、わかりません, "however many times I hear it, I don't understand". With a question word it means "no matter what, who, how": 何を食べても.
entries.why: The て-form joins A to B, and も, "even", marks A as something that might have been expected to change B but does not. So the sentence says B survives even A. With a question word, "even whatever" becomes "no matter what". い-adjectives use their て-form (高くても); nouns and な-adjectives use でも (雨でも, 静かでも). This でも is the same pattern, not the word でも that starts a sentence to mean "but".

formation.note: 降っても, 食べても, しても. Negative: なくても (OJG-0067).
高くても; いい → よくても.
雨でも, 静かでも.

examples.japanese: 雨が降っても、サッカーの練習はあります。
examples.reading: あめがふっても、サッカーのれんしゅうはあります。
examples.romaji: ame ga futte mo, sakkā no renshū wa arimasu.
examples.english: Even if it rains, there's football practice.

examples.japanese: 何回聞いても、わかりません。
examples.reading: なんかいきいても、わかりません。
examples.romaji: nankai kiite mo, wakarimasen.
examples.english: No matter how many times I hear it, I don't understand.

examples.japanese: 高くても、このかばんを買いたいです。
examples.reading: たかくても、このかばんをかいたいです。
examples.romaji: takakute mo, kono kaban o kaitai desu.
examples.english: Even if it's expensive, I want to buy this bag.

examples.japanese: 日曜日でも、店は開いています。
examples.reading: にちようびでも、みせはあいています。
examples.romaji: nichiyōbi demo, mise wa aite imasu.
examples.english: The shop is open even on Sundays.

mistake.wrong: 寒いても、毎朝走ります。
mistake.problem: An い-adjective forms ても from its て-form, 寒くて, so it is 寒くても.
mistake.right: 寒くても、毎朝走ります。

distinguish_from.note: のに is for a fact that turned out against expectation, often with frustration. ても covers hypotheses too, and is neutral.

entries.title: If, when (once A has happened)
entries.meaning: た-form + ら: "if A" or "when A (has happened)"; B follows once A is realised.
entries.when: Use it for a condition (もし雨が降ったら, "if it rains") and for "when, once" about something sure to happen (駅に着いたら電話します, "I'll call when I get to the station"). It is the most widely usable conditional in speech and works before requests, invitations and intentions. With a past-tense B, it tells what you found when you did A: 窓を開けたら、雪が降っていました.
entries.why: たら is built on the past form: A is pictured as already done, and B is what happens from that point on. That is why it covers both "if", when A may not happen, and "when", when A surely will, and why B follows A in time. It is also why a request or an intention fits after it: B is meant to come once A is done. With a past-tense B, it describes a discovery, something you found or that happened once A was done.

formation.note: 行ったら, 食べたら, したら, 来たら; negative 行かなかったら.
高かったら; いい → よかったら.
雨だったら, ひまだったら.

examples.japanese: 駅に着いたら、電話してください。
examples.reading: えきについたら、でんわしてください。
examples.romaji: eki ni tsuitara, denwa shite kudasai.
examples.english: When you get to the station, please call me.

examples.japanese: もし雨が降ったら、試合は中止です。
examples.reading: もしあめがふったら、しあいはちゅうしです。
examples.romaji: moshi ame ga futtara, shiai wa chūshi desu.
examples.english: If it rains, the match will be cancelled.

examples.japanese: 窓を開けたら、雪が降っていました。
examples.reading: まどをあけたら、ゆきがふっていました。
examples.romaji: mado o aketara, yuki ga futte imashita.
examples.english: When I opened the window, it was snowing.

examples.japanese: よかったら、いっしょに食べませんか。
examples.reading: よかったら、いっしょにたべませんか。
examples.romaji: yokattara, issho ni tabemasen ka.
examples.english: If you'd like, shall we eat together?

mistake.wrong: 旅行に行ったら、ガイドブックを買います。
mistake.problem: Meant as "I'll buy a guidebook before the trip". たら puts B after A, so this says you will buy it once you are on the trip. For something done beforehand, use なら.
mistake.right: 旅行に行くなら、ガイドブックを買います。

distinguish_from.note: ば focuses on A as the condition and avoids requests after an action. たら puts B after A and takes requests and intentions freely.
と is for results that follow automatically, and B cannot be a request or wish. たら has no such limit.
なら takes A as given and says what applies, whatever the order in time. たら needs A to happen first.

entries.title: Don't have to, needn't
entries.meaning: V-なくてもいい: "you don't have to V"; it is fine not to do V.
entries.when: Use it to say something is not necessary, or to ask whether you can skip it: 明日は来なくてもいいです, "you don't have to come tomorrow"; 靴を脱がなくてもいいですか, "do I need to take my shoes off?". It is the "no" answer to a question with なければなりませんか. Politer: なくても大丈夫です, なくてもかまいません.
entries.why: It is ても, "even if", plus いい, "fine": "even if you don't V, it's fine". So it gives permission not to act, the negative partner of てもいい. It does not forbid anything: 来なくてもいい still allows you to come. For "must not", use てはいけない.

formation.form: V (ない-form, drop い) + くてもいい
formation.note: 行かなくてもいい, 食べなくてもいい, しなくてもいい, 来なくてもいい. Polite: いいです.

examples.japanese: 明日は来なくてもいいですよ。
examples.reading: あしたはこなくてもいいですよ。
examples.romaji: ashita wa konakute mo ii desu yo.
examples.english: You don't have to come tomorrow.

examples.japanese: ここでは靴を脱がなくてもいいです。
examples.reading: ここではくつをぬがなくてもいいです。
examples.romaji: koko de wa kutsu o nuganakute mo ii desu.
examples.english: You don't need to take your shoes off here.

examples.japanese: 「全部食べなければいけませんか。」「いいえ、全部食べなくてもいいですよ。」
examples.reading: 「ぜんぶたべなければいけませんか。」「いいえ、ぜんぶたべなくてもいいですよ。」
examples.romaji: "zenbu tabenakereba ikemasen ka." "iie, zenbu tabenakute mo ii desu yo."
examples.english: "Do I have to eat all of it?" "No, you don't have to eat it all."

mistake.wrong: ここで写真を撮らなくてもいいです。
mistake.problem: Meant as "you mustn't take photos here". なくてもいい only says it is not necessary. A prohibition is てはいけません.
mistake.right: ここで写真を撮ってはいけません。

distinguish_from.note: てもいい permits doing something. なくてもいい permits not doing it.
なければならない says you must. なくてもいい says you don't have to.

entries.title: Seems like, looks like; like (a comparison)
entries.meaning: ～みたいだ: "it seems / looks like…", judged from evidence; after a noun, also "like N". Conversational.
entries.when: Use it in conversation for a guess based on what you have seen or heard: 田中さんは風邪をひいたみたいです, "it seems Tanaka-san has caught a cold". After a noun, it also compares (ぬいぐるみみたいにかわいい, "cute as a stuffed toy") and gives an example (東京みたいな大きい町, "a big city like Tokyo"). It is the conversational counterpart of ようだ.
entries.why: みたい grew out of 見たよう, "as if seen": the speaker reads the situation from evidence instead of stating it as fact. So it follows complete statements in plain form, and it is softer than a flat statement. Unlike ようだ, it joins nouns and な-adjectives directly, with no の, な or だ: 雨みたい, 元気みたい. It behaves like a な-adjective itself: みたいな before a noun, みたいに before a verb or adjective, みたいだ／みたいです at the end.

formation.form: Verb / い-adjective (plain form) + みたい
formation.note: 降るみたい, 降ったみたい, 高いみたい.
No だ: 雨みたい, 静かみたい.

formation.form: みたいな + noun; みたいに + verb or adjective

examples.japanese: 田中さんは風邪をひいたみたいです。
examples.reading: たなかさんはかぜをひいたみたいです。
examples.romaji: tanaka-san wa kaze o hiita mitai desu.
examples.english: It seems Tanaka-san has caught a cold.

examples.japanese: 外は雨みたいですね。
examples.reading: そとはあめみたいですね。
examples.romaji: soto wa ame mitai desu ne.
examples.english: It looks like it's raining outside.

examples.japanese: この犬は、ぬいぐるみみたいにかわいい。
examples.reading: このいぬは、ぬいぐるみみたいにかわいい。
examples.romaji: kono inu wa, nuigurumi mitai ni kawaii.
examples.english: This dog is as cute as a stuffed toy.

examples.japanese: 東京みたいな大きい町に住みたいです。
examples.reading: とうきょうみたいなおおきいまちにすみたいです。
examples.romaji: tōkyō mitai na ōkii machi ni sumitai desu.
examples.english: I want to live in a big city like Tokyo.

mistake.wrong: あの人は学生だみたいです。
mistake.problem: After a noun or な-adjective, みたい follows directly, without だ.
mistake.right: あの人は学生みたいです。

distinguish_from.note: ようだ means the same but is more formal and needs の after a noun and な after a な-adjective (学生のようだ, 静かなようだ). みたい joins them directly.
そう after a stem gives an impression from appearance before you know (おいしそう). みたい draws a conclusion from evidence (おいしいみたい, "it seems to be good", perhaps from what others say).

entries.title: Doing something completely, or regrettably
entries.meaning: V-てしまう: V is done completely, or happened with regret or by accident. Casual: ちゃう／じゃう.
entries.when: Use it for two things: to say an action is finished completely (宿題を全部やってしまった, "I've finished all my homework"), and, very often, to show that something happened that you regret or did not mean to happen (傘を忘れてしまいました, "I (unfortunately) left my umbrella behind"). In speech, てしまう becomes ちゃう and でしまう becomes じゃう: 食べちゃった, 飲んじゃった.
entries.why: しまう means "put away, close up". After the て-form it says the action is closed up, done for good. When the result is something you would rather not have, "done, and it can't be undone" turns into regret: 忘れてしまった says you forgot, and it is too late. Context decides which reading you get: a chore finished, or a mistake made. It only adds the speaker's view of the event; without it, 傘を忘れました states the bare fact.

formation.note: Polite: てしまいます, てしまいました.
Casual: 食べちゃう, 忘れちゃった; 飲んじゃう, 読んじゃった.

examples.japanese: 電車に傘を忘れてしまいました。
examples.reading: でんしゃにかさをわすれてしまいました。
examples.romaji: densha ni kasa o wasurete shimaimashita.
examples.english: I left my umbrella on the train.

examples.japanese: 宿題はもう全部やってしまいました。
examples.reading: しゅくだいはもうぜんぶやってしまいました。
examples.romaji: shukudai wa mō zenbu yatte shimaimashita.
examples.english: I've already finished all my homework.

examples.japanese: ケーキを全部食べちゃった。
examples.reading: ケーキをぜんぶたべちゃった。
examples.romaji: kēki o zenbu tabechatta.
examples.english: I ate the whole cake. (Oops.)

mistake.wrong: 試験に合格してしまいました。
mistake.problem: Meant as good news. てしまう colours an event as regrettable or unintended, so this sounds as if passing were a misfortune. Say it plainly.
mistake.right: 試験に合格しました。

entries.title: When A, B follows (as a matter of course)
entries.meaning: Plain non-past + と: "when/whenever A, B"; B follows naturally or automatically from A.
entries.when: Use it when B always or automatically follows A: 春になると、桜が咲きます, "when spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom"; このボタンを押すと、お湯が出ます. It also gives directions (まっすぐ行くと、右に郵便局があります) and, with a past-tense B, tells what you found when you did A (家に帰ると、姉が来ていました).
entries.why: と links A and B as a fixed sequence: whenever A happens, B comes with it. Because B follows by itself, it cannot be something the speaker wants, asks for or intends: a request, invitation, ましょう or たい after と sounds wrong. A stays in the non-past plain form even in a story about the past, because the tense is carried by B: 家に帰ると、…いました.

formation.note: 押すと, 押さないと; 寒いと.
雨だと, 静かだと.

examples.japanese: 春になると、桜が咲きます。
examples.reading: はるになると、さくらがさきます。
examples.romaji: haru ni naru to, sakura ga sakimasu.
examples.english: When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.

examples.japanese: このボタンを押すと、お湯が出ます。
examples.reading: このボタンをおすと、おゆがでます。
examples.romaji: kono botan o osu to, oyu ga demasu.
examples.english: When you press this button, hot water comes out.

examples.japanese: まっすぐ行くと、右に郵便局があります。
examples.reading: まっすぐいくと、みぎにゆうびんきょくがあります。
examples.romaji: massugu iku to, migi ni yūbinkyoku ga arimasu.
examples.english: If you go straight on, there's a post office on the right.

examples.japanese: 家に帰ると、姉が来ていました。
examples.reading: いえにかえると、あねがきていました。
examples.romaji: ie ni kaeru to, ane ga kite imashita.
examples.english: When I got home, my older sister was there.
examples.note: A past B tells what the speaker found. A stays non-past.

mistake.wrong: 駅に着くと、電話してください。
mistake.problem: With と, B follows A by itself, so B cannot be a request. Use たら.
mistake.right: 駅に着いたら、電話してください。

distinguish_from.note: たら allows requests, wishes and intentions after it. と does not.
ば focuses on A as a condition to be met. と presents B as what naturally comes with A.

entries.title: While doing (two actions at once)
entries.meaning: V (ます-stem) + ながら: "while V-ing"; one person does two actions at once, the main one coming last.
entries.when: Use it when the same person does two things at the same time: 音楽を聞きながら勉強します, "I study while listening to music". The action before ながら is in the background; the one after it is the main action.
entries.why: ながら turns the first verb into a background activity that runs alongside the main one. The tense and politeness of the whole sentence come from the last verb, so the verb before ながら is always the ます-stem, whatever the tense: 聞きながら勉強しました. Because the two actions belong to one person, ながら cannot join two people's actions; for "while she cooked, I…", use 間 (あいだ). The order matters: the main action goes last, so 勉強しながら音楽を聞く makes the music the point.

formation.note: 聞く → 聞きながら, 食べる → 食べながら, 歩く → 歩きながら.

examples.japanese: 音楽を聞きながら勉強します。
examples.reading: おんがくをききながらべんきょうします。
examples.romaji: ongaku o kikinagara benkyō shimasu.
examples.english: I study while listening to music.

examples.japanese: 歩きながらスマホを見ないでください。
examples.reading: あるきながらスマホをみないでください。
examples.romaji: arukinagara sumaho o minaide kudasai.
examples.english: Please don't look at your phone while walking.

examples.japanese: 父はテレビを見ながらご飯を食べます。
examples.reading: ちちはテレビをみながらごはんをたべます。
examples.romaji: chichi wa terebi o minagara gohan o tabemasu.
examples.english: My father eats while watching TV.

mistake.wrong: 母が料理を作りながら、私はテレビを見ていました。
mistake.problem: ながら joins two actions of the same person. For two people doing things at the same time, use 間.
mistake.right: 母が料理を作っている間、私はテレビを見ていました。

distinguish_from.note: 間 and 間に can join the actions of two different people, and 間に sets a point within the period. ながら is one person doing two things at once.

entries.title: I should have… (regret)
entries.meaning: V-ばよかった: "I should have V-ed", "if only I had V-ed"; regret about something that did not happen.
entries.when: Use it to regret something you did not do: 傘を持ってくればよかった, "I should have brought an umbrella". With the negative, it regrets something you did: 食べなければよかった, "I shouldn't have eaten it". It often ends in なあ, as a sigh. たらよかった is used the same way.
entries.why: ば sets a condition and よかった says "it would have been good": "if I had done V, it would have been good". That implies you did not do it, so the sentence is regret. よかった is past because the chance has already gone. Said about someone else, it becomes criticism: もっと早く言えばよかったのに, "you should have said so sooner".

formation.note: 持ってくればよかった, 行けばよかった. Polite: よかったです.

formation.form: V (negative ば-form, なければ) + よかった
formation.note: 食べなければよかった, "I shouldn't have eaten it".

examples.japanese: 傘を持ってくればよかった。
examples.reading: かさをもってくればよかった。
examples.romaji: kasa o motte kureba yokatta.
examples.english: I should have brought an umbrella.

examples.japanese: もっと早く家を出ればよかったです。
examples.reading: もっとはやくいえをでればよかったです。
examples.romaji: motto hayaku ie o dereba yokatta desu.
examples.english: I should have left home earlier.

examples.japanese: あんなに食べなければよかった。
examples.reading: あんなにたべなければよかった。
examples.romaji: anna ni tabenakereba yokatta.
examples.english: I shouldn't have eaten so much.

mistake.wrong: もっと勉強すればいいでした。
mistake.problem: The past of いい is よかった. いいでした is not a form.
mistake.right: もっと勉強すればよかったです。

distinguish_from.note: ばいい is advice about what to do now or next (どうすればいいですか). ばよかった looks back at a chance that has gone.
てよかった is glad about what did happen. ばよかった regrets what did not.

entries.title: Thank you for doing…
entries.meaning: V-てくれてありがとう: "thank you for V-ing (for me)"; thanks someone for a specific kindness.
entries.when: Use it to thank someone for something they did for you: 手伝ってくれてありがとう, "thanks for helping me". Politely: てくれてありがとうございます, or ございました when it is over. To a superior, use くださって: 教えてくださってありがとうございました.
entries.why: てくれる marks the action as a favour done for you, and its て-form gives the reason for the thanks: "you did V for me, and so, thank you". What you are thanking for is the favour, so くれて is needed; 手伝ってありがとう leaves it out and sounds wrong. For someone above you, the honorific くださって takes the place of くれて.

formation.form: V (て-form) + くれて + ありがとう
formation.note: Polite: ありがとうございます／ございました.

formation.form: V (て-form) + くださって + ありがとうございます
formation.note: To a superior.

examples.japanese: 手伝ってくれてありがとう。
examples.reading: てつだってくれてありがとう。
examples.romaji: tetsudatte kurete arigatō.
examples.english: Thanks for helping me.

examples.japanese: 来てくれて、本当にありがとう。
examples.reading: きてくれて、ほんとうにありがとう。
examples.romaji: kite kurete, hontō ni arigatō.
examples.english: Thank you so much for coming.

examples.japanese: 先生、いろいろ教えてくださってありがとうございました。
examples.reading: せんせい、いろいろおしえてくださってありがとうございました。
examples.romaji: sensei, iroiro oshiete kudasatte arigatō gozaimashita.
examples.english: Thank you for teaching me so much, sensei.

mistake.wrong: 手伝ってありがとう。
mistake.problem: The thanks is for a favour, so the action needs くれて, which marks it as done for you.
mistake.right: 手伝ってくれてありがとう。

distinguish_from.note: てくれる is the favour itself. てくれてありがとう thanks the person for it.

review.note: A set use of てくれる (OJG-0056); kept as its own entry because both source lists have it.

entries.title: I'm glad that…
entries.meaning: V-てよかった: "I'm glad (that) V", "it's good that V"; relief or pleasure at how something turned out.
entries.when: Use it for something that happened and turned out well: 日本に来てよかったです, "I'm glad I came to Japan"; 間に合ってよかった, "thank goodness we made it". For something that did not happen, use なくて: 雨が降らなくてよかった.
entries.why: The て-form gives the cause and よかった gives the verdict: "V happened, and so it was good". よかった is past because it judges something that has already come about. The negative takes なくて, the negative て-form that gives a reason. Compare ばよかった, which is about what did not happen (regret); てよかった is about what did (relief).

formation.note: 来てよかった, 間に合ってよかった; negative 降らなくてよかった.

formation.form: い-adjective (くて) / noun or な-adjective (で) + よかった
formation.note: 安くてよかった, 元気でよかった.

examples.japanese: 日本に来てよかったです。
examples.reading: にほんにきてよかったです。
examples.romaji: nihon ni kite yokatta desu.
examples.english: I'm glad I came to Japan.

examples.japanese: 雨が降らなくてよかったですね。
examples.reading: あめがふらなくてよかったですね。
examples.romaji: ame ga furanakute yokatta desu ne.
examples.english: It's good it didn't rain, isn't it.

examples.japanese: みんな元気でよかった。
examples.reading: みんなげんきでよかった。
examples.romaji: minna genki de yokatta.
examples.english: I'm glad everyone is well.

mistake.wrong: 試験に合格すればよかったです。
mistake.problem: Meant as "I'm glad I passed". ばよかった means "I should have passed", regret about something that did not happen. For relief about what did happen, use てよかった.
mistake.right: 試験に合格してよかったです。

distinguish_from.note: ばよかった regrets what did not happen. てよかった is glad about what did.

entries.title: Should be, is supposed to (a confident inference)
entries.meaning: Plain form + はずです: "should", "is supposed to"; a confident expectation drawn from what the speaker knows.
entries.when: Use it when you have grounds to expect something: 田中さんは三時に来るはずです, "Tanaka-san should be coming at three" (he said so). With a past form, for something that should already be the case: もう着いたはずです. はずがない means "there's no way that…".
entries.why: はず is a noun meaning "what is to be expected". The sentence says the thing follows from facts the speaker knows: a timetable, a promise, a rule, simple logic. So it is more confident than でしょう or かもしれない, but it is still an inference, and if it turns out wrong, the speaker is surprised (はずなのに). As a noun, はず is joined like one: の after a noun (休みのはず), な after a な-adjective (静かなはず), and plain forms after verbs and い-adjectives. It is not for your own intentions; for plans, use つもり.

formation.note: 来るはず, 来たはず, 来ないはず; 高いはず.

formation.form: な-adjective + な + はず; Noun + の + はず
formation.note: 静かなはず, 休みのはず.
"There's no way": 田中さんが知っているはずがない.

examples.japanese: 田中さんは三時に来るはずです。
examples.reading: たなかさんはさんじにくるはずです。
examples.romaji: tanaka-san wa sanji ni kuru hazu desu.
examples.english: Tanaka-san should be coming at three.

examples.japanese: 荷物は昨日送ったので、もう着いたはずです。
examples.reading: にもつはきのうおくったので、もうついたはずです。
examples.romaji: nimotsu wa kinō okutta node, mō tsuita hazu desu.
examples.english: I sent the parcel yesterday, so it should have arrived by now.

examples.japanese: 今日は日曜日だから、銀行は休みのはずです。
examples.reading: きょうはにちようびだから、ぎんこうはやすみのはずです。
examples.romaji: kyō wa nichiyōbi da kara, ginkō wa yasumi no hazu desu.
examples.english: It's Sunday, so the bank should be closed.

mistake.wrong: 私は来年日本に行くはずです。
mistake.problem: Meant as "I intend to go". はず is an inference from facts, not an intention. For your own plan, use つもり.
mistake.right: 私は来年日本に行くつもりです。

distinguish_from.note: つもり is your own intention. はず is what you expect, reasoning from facts.
でしょう is a guess. はず is a confident expectation with grounds behind it.

entries.title: Without doing, instead of doing
entries.meaning: V-ないで: "without V-ing", or "instead of V-ing"; says how the next action is done.
entries.when: Use it to say an action is done without another one: 朝ご飯を食べないで家を出ました, "I left home without eating breakfast". It can also mean "instead of": バスに乗らないで歩きました, "I walked instead of taking the bus".
entries.why: ないで is the negative partner of the て-form that describes the manner of the next action: 傘を持って出かける, "go out taking an umbrella", and 傘を持たないで出かける, "go out without an umbrella". It says how the main action is done, so both parts belong to the same person. A negative reason ("because it didn't…") is made with なくて instead: 雨が降らなくて困っています.

formation.note: 食べないで, 行かないで, しないで, 来ないで.

examples.japanese: 今朝は朝ご飯を食べないで家を出ました。
examples.reading: けさはあさごはんをたべないでいえをでました。
examples.romaji: kesa wa asagohan o tabenaide ie o demashita.
examples.english: This morning I left home without eating breakfast.

examples.japanese: 辞書を使わないで読んでみてください。
examples.reading: じしょをつかわないでよんでみてください。
examples.romaji: jisho o tsukawanaide yonde mite kudasai.
examples.english: Try reading it without using a dictionary.

examples.japanese: 今日はバスに乗らないで、駅まで歩きました。
examples.reading: きょうはバスにのらないで、えきまであるきました。
examples.romaji: kyō wa basu ni noranaide, eki made arukimashita.
examples.english: Today I walked to the station instead of taking the bus.

mistake.wrong: 雨が降らないで、困っています。
mistake.problem: The first part is the reason for the trouble, and a negative reason takes なくて. ないで says how an action is done, "without", which does not fit here.
mistake.right: 雨が降らなくて、困っています。

distinguish_from.note: ないでください asks someone not to do something. ないで on its own joins "without doing A" to the next action.

entries.title: Whether or not
entries.meaning: Plain form + かどうか: "whether (or not)"; puts a yes-no question inside a larger sentence.
entries.when: Use it when a yes-no question becomes part of a bigger sentence: 明日行けるかどうか、わかりません, "I don't know whether I can go tomorrow". It is common with わかる, 知る, 聞く, 調べる and 考える. A question with a question word takes only か: 何時に始まるか知っていますか.
entries.why: か marks a question, and どうか is "or how (not)". So かどうか says "whether it is so or not", and turns a yes-no question into a chunk that the main verb can take like a noun. As a question tucked inside a sentence, it uses plain forms, and a noun or な-adjective drops だ (本当かどうか), as it does in a plain question. With a question word there is no yes-or-no choice to make, so only か is used.

formation.form: Verb / い-adjective (plain form) + かどうか
formation.note: 行けるかどうか, 来たかどうか; 新しいかどうか.
No だ: 本当かどうか, 大丈夫かどうか.

examples.japanese: 明日のパーティーに行けるかどうか、まだわかりません。
examples.reading: あしたのパーティーにいけるかどうか、まだわかりません。
examples.romaji: ashita no pātī ni ikeru ka dō ka, mada wakarimasen.
examples.english: I don't know yet whether I can go to tomorrow's party.

examples.japanese: この魚が新しいかどうか、店の人に聞きました。
examples.reading: このさかながあたらしいかどうか、みせのひとにききました。
examples.romaji: kono sakana ga atarashii ka dō ka, mise no hito ni kikimashita.
examples.english: I asked the shop staff whether this fish was fresh.

examples.japanese: その話が本当かどうか、調べてみます。
examples.reading: そのはなしがほんとうかどうか、しらべてみます。
examples.romaji: sono hanashi ga hontō ka dō ka, shirabete mimasu.
examples.english: I'll check whether that story is true.

mistake.wrong: 会議が何時に始まるかどうか知っていますか。
mistake.problem: With a question word (何時), the question is not yes-or-no, so only か is used.
mistake.right: 会議が何時に始まるか知っていますか。

distinguish_from.note: A question word + か embeds an open question (何時に始まるか). かどうか embeds a yes-no question.

entries.title: Called, named; the (news) that…
entries.meaning: X という N: "an N called X"; also joins content to nouns like 話 or ニュース, "the news that…". Casual: っていう.
entries.when: Use it to name or introduce something the listener may not know: 「さくら」という店, "a shop called Sakura"; 山田という人, "someone named Yamada". Ask a name with 何という: これは何という花ですか. It also joins what something says to a noun of information: 来週テストがあるという話, "talk that there's a test next week". Casual speech uses っていう or って.
entries.why: と marks a quotation and いう is "say", so X という N is "an N one calls X". That is why it introduces unfamiliar names: you give the label the thing goes by, and it would sound odd for something everyone already knows. The same logic lets a whole sentence be the content of a noun like 話, ニュース or うわさ, the thing that says it. In these uses いう is usually written in kana.

formation.note: 「さくら」という店, 山田という人. Question: 何という + noun.
With nouns of information such as 話, ニュース, うわさ, 手紙.
Casual.
