examples.reading: 「さくら」というみせをしっていますか。
examples.romaji: "sakura" to iu mise o shitte imasu ka.
examples.english: Do you know a shop called Sakura?

examples.japanese: これは何という花ですか。
examples.reading: これはなんというはなですか。
examples.romaji: kore wa nan to iu hana desu ka.
examples.english: What is this flower called?

examples.japanese: 来週テストがあるという話を聞きました。
examples.reading: らいしゅうテストがあるというはなしをききました。
examples.romaji: raishū tesuto ga aru to iu hanashi o kikimashita.
examples.english: I heard that there's a test next week.

examples.japanese: 山田っていう人から電話があったよ。
examples.reading: やまだっていうひとからでんわがあったよ。
examples.romaji: yamada tte iu hito kara denwa ga atta yo.
examples.english: Someone called Yamada phoned you.

mistake.wrong: 私は東京という町に住んでいます。
mistake.problem: Said to a Japanese listener. という introduces a name the listener may not know, so using it for Tokyo sounds as if they had never heard of it. Name a well-known place directly.
mistake.right: 私は東京に住んでいます。

distinguish_from.note: なんと言いますか asks what something is called in a language. 何という + noun asks the name of a particular thing.

entries.title: Easy to do
entries.meaning: V (ます-stem) + やすい: "easy to V"; with things that just happen, "tends to V".
entries.when: Use it for something that is easy to do because of what it is like: このペンは書きやすい, "this pen is easy to write with"; 先生の説明はわかりやすい. With verbs for things that happen by themselves, it means "tends to, is prone to": 冬は風邪をひきやすい, このコップは割れやすい.
entries.why: やすい means "easy". Joined to a verb's ます-stem, it makes a new い-adjective: 読みやすい, "easy-to-read", which conjugates like any い-adjective (読みやすかった, 読みやすくない, 読みやすい本). The subject is usually the thing the action is done to or with, not the person doing it: この本は読みやすい. When the verb is something that happens by itself (割れる, 忘れる), "easy to happen" means "tends to happen". This やすい is not 安い, "cheap", which only sounds the same.

formation.note: 書く → 書きやすい, 食べる → 食べやすい, わかる → わかりやすい. Conjugates as an い-adjective.

examples.japanese: この靴は軽くて歩きやすいです。
examples.reading: このくつはかるくてあるきやすいです。
examples.romaji: kono kutsu wa karukute arukiyasui desu.
examples.english: These shoes are light and easy to walk in.

examples.japanese: 先生の説明はわかりやすいです。
examples.reading: せんせいのせつめいはわかりやすいです。
examples.romaji: sensei no setsumei wa wakariyasui desu.
examples.english: The teacher's explanations are easy to understand.

examples.japanese: 冬は風邪をひきやすいです。
examples.reading: ふゆはかぜをひきやすいです。
examples.romaji: fuyu wa kaze o hikiyasui desu.
examples.english: It's easy to catch a cold in winter.
examples.note: A thing that happens to you, so "tends to" rather than "easy to do".

mistake.wrong: この本は読むやすいです。
mistake.problem: やすい joins the ます-stem (読み), not the dictionary form.
mistake.right: この本は読みやすいです。

distinguish_from.note: にくい is the opposite, "hard to V", and is formed the same way.

entries.title: Hard to do
entries.meaning: V (ます-stem) + にくい: "hard to V"; with things that happen, "doesn't easily V".
entries.when: Use it for something that is hard to do because of what it is like: この肉は硬くて食べにくい, "this meat is tough and hard to eat"; 字が小さくて読みにくい. With verbs for things that happen, it means "doesn't easily happen", which can be a good thing: 割れにくいコップ, "a glass that doesn't break easily".
entries.why: にくい means "hard to". Like やすい, it joins the ます-stem and makes an い-adjective: 読みにくい, 読みにくかった, 読みにくい字. It describes a thing by how hard it makes an action, so the subject is usually the thing, not the person. For a task that is simply difficult, such as a hard question, use 難しい instead: この問題は難しい.

formation.note: 読む → 読みにくい, 食べる → 食べにくい, 割れる → 割れにくい. Conjugates as an い-adjective.

examples.japanese: この肉は硬くて、食べにくいです。
examples.reading: このにくはかたくて、たべにくいです。
examples.romaji: kono niku wa katakute, tabenikui desu.
examples.english: This meat is tough and hard to eat.

examples.japanese: 字が小さくて読みにくいです。
examples.reading: じがちいさくてよみにくいです。
examples.romaji: ji ga chiisakute yominikui desu.
examples.english: The writing is small and hard to read.

examples.japanese: このコップは割れにくいです。
examples.reading: このコップはわれにくいです。
examples.romaji: kono koppu wa warenikui desu.
examples.english: This glass doesn't break easily.

mistake.wrong: この道は歩くにくいです。
mistake.problem: にくい joins the ます-stem (歩き), not the dictionary form.
mistake.right: この道は歩きにくいです。

distinguish_from.note: やすい is the opposite, "easy to V", and is formed the same way.

entries.title: Having something done to you (the passive)
entries.meaning: Passive V-られる／V-れる: the subject is the one the action happens to; the doer, if named, takes に.
entries.when: Use it to tell an event from the side of the one it happened to: 弟は先生にほめられました, "my brother was praised by the teacher". It is also used when the doer is unknown or unimportant, as in news and descriptions (このお寺は八百年前に建てられました), and for being troubled by something: 雨に降られました, "I got caught in the rain".
entries.why: The passive moves the one affected into the subject and the doer to に: 先生が弟をほめた becomes 弟は先生にほめられた. Japanese likes to keep the story on the speaker's side, so when something happens to you, the passive lets you stay the subject: 私は友だちに笑われた. Because the one affected is the subject, even an intransitive event can be passive when it troubles someone (雨に降られた). When something is done to a part of you or to your belongings, the person is the subject and the part keeps を: 足を踏まれた.

formation.note: 書く → 書かれる, 読む → 読まれる, 言う → 言われる, 踏む → 踏まれる.
食べる → 食べられる, ほめる → ほめられる. This looks the same as the potential form; context tells them apart.

formation.form: する → される; 来る → 来られる (こられる)
formation.note: The passive is itself an ichidan verb (ほめられます, ほめられた).

examples.japanese: 弟は先生にほめられました。
examples.reading: おとうとはせんせいにほめられました。
examples.romaji: otōto wa sensei ni homeraremashita.
examples.english: My little brother was praised by the teacher.

examples.japanese: 電車の中で足を踏まれました。
examples.reading: でんしゃのなかであしをふまれました。
examples.romaji: densha no naka de ashi o fumaremashita.
examples.english: Someone stepped on my foot on the train.

examples.japanese: このお寺は八百年前に建てられました。
examples.reading: このおてらははっぴゃくねんまえにたてられました。
examples.romaji: kono otera wa happyakunen mae ni tateraremashita.
examples.english: This temple was built 800 years ago.

examples.japanese: 帰り道で雨に降られました。
examples.reading: かえりみちであめにふられました。
examples.romaji: kaerimichi de ame ni furaremashita.
examples.english: I got caught in the rain on the way home.
examples.note: An intransitive verb in the passive, because the rain troubled the speaker.

mistake.wrong: 私の足は電車の中で踏まれました。
mistake.problem: When something is done to a part of you, Japanese makes the person the subject and keeps the part as the object with を.
mistake.right: 私は電車の中で足を踏まれました。

distinguish_from.note: させられる is the passive of the causative, "be made to do". られる on its own is "have something done to you".

review.note: Tanos 525 lists only ～られる; this entry reads it as the passive. The potential form (食べられる, "can eat") shares the ichidan shape but has no entry of its own at N4. Should it get one?

entries.title: Something has been done on purpose, and the result remains
entries.meaning: V-てある: someone did V on purpose, and its result or its preparation remains.
entries.when: Use it to describe the state a thing is in because someone did something to it on purpose and left it that way, often in preparation for later: the plates are set out, the window has been opened, a name has been written. The focus is on the result, not on who did it. A related use says that something has been done in advance: もう切符を買ってあります, "I have already bought the tickets".
entries.why: ある says that a thing is there. After the て-form of a verb, it says the result of that action is there: 置いてある is "placed, and there". In this result-state use, the thing acted on is usually marked with が, or with は when it is already the topic; the verb is normally transitive and describes a deliberate action; and the doer is usually left unsaid, because the sentence is about the result. In the preparation use, the verb keeps its ordinary particles, including を, and the doer can be named: 私は切符を買ってある. A few deliberate intransitive verbs also appear in this use, as in 十分休んである, "I have rested enough in advance".

formation.form: thing が／は … V (transitive, て-form) + ある
formation.note: The result-state use. Polite: V-てあります. The helper is always ある, never いる.

The preparation use: an action has been completed in advance. The verb keeps its ordinary particles, including を for the object of a transitive verb. Some deliberate intransitive verbs also occur here, as in 十分休んである.

examples.japanese: 本は机の上に置いてあります。
examples.reading: ほんはつくえのうえにおいてあります。
examples.english: The book has been put on the desk.

examples.japanese: テーブルの上にお皿が置いてあります。
examples.reading: テーブルのうえにおさらがおいてあります。
examples.english: Plates have been set out on the table.

examples.japanese: ここに名前が書いてあります。
examples.reading: ここになまえがかいてあります。
examples.english: A name has been written here.

examples.japanese: もう切符を買ってあります。
examples.reading: もうきっぷをかってあります。
examples.english: I have already bought the tickets.
examples.note: The preparation use: を stays, and the doer is the speaker.

mistake.wrong: 窓が開いてあります。
mistake.problem: In the result-state use, てある needs a transitive verb that expresses someone acting on the thing. Intransitive 開く presents the window’s change without expressing anyone acting on it. Use transitive 開ける to say someone opened it on purpose, or 開いている for the plain state.
mistake.right: 窓が開けてあります。

distinguish_from.note: With a verb of change, ている describes the state (窓が開いている). てある presents a deliberate action as done, with its result or preparation remaining (窓が開けてある). ている can also describe an action in progress; てある does not.

review.note: Adapted from the Mieru Nihongo note on 〜てあります, which two models agreed on (2026-09-21), and rewritten to stand on its own. The rewrite is new text, so it starts again at draft. The を〜てある variant (窓を開けてある) is left out on purpose; it wants its own careful note.

reviews.note: The entry accurately distinguishes the result-state and preparation uses of ～てある. The formations, examples, readings, translations, mistake correction, and comparison with ～ている are correct, and N4 is plausible.

entries.title: While (something happens during a period)
entries.meaning: V-ている間に, N の間に: "while…", "during…"; something happens at some point within that period.
entries.when: Use it when one event happens at some point during a period marked by another action or state: 母が寝ている間に、部屋を掃除しました, "while my mother was asleep, I cleaned the room". With a noun: 夏休みの間に. The two parts can have different subjects. Without に, 間 means "the whole time": 待っている間、ずっと本を読んでいました.
entries.why: 間 (あいだ) is "the space between", here a stretch of time. With に, it marks a point inside that stretch where something happens, the same に as in 三時に. Without に, the stretch itself is the time, so the main part describes something that lasts all the way through it, usually in the ている form or with ずっと. The period is a state, so a verb before 間 is usually in the ている form, or a verb of state such as いる.

formation.note: Something happens at some point within the period.
夏休みの間に, 留守の間に.

formation.form: V (ている) / Noun + の + 間
formation.note: Without に, for something that lasts through the whole period.

examples.japanese: 母が寝ている間に、部屋を掃除しました。
examples.reading: ははがねているあいだに、へやをそうじしました。
examples.romaji: haha ga nete iru aida ni, heya o sōji shimashita.
examples.english: While my mother was asleep, I cleaned the room.

examples.japanese: 夏休みの間に、運転免許を取りたいです。
examples.reading: なつやすみのあいだに、うんてんめんきょをとりたいです。
examples.romaji: natsuyasumi no aida ni, unten menkyo o toritai desu.
examples.english: I want to get my driving licence during the summer holidays.

examples.japanese: 電車を待っている間、ずっと本を読んでいました。
examples.reading: でんしゃをまっているあいだ、ずっとほんをよんでいました。
examples.romaji: densha o matte iru aida, zutto hon o yonde imashita.
examples.english: The whole time I was waiting for the train, I was reading.
examples.note: No に, because the reading lasted through the whole wait.

mistake.wrong: 電車を待っている間に、ずっと本を読んでいました。
mistake.problem: ずっと says the reading lasted the whole time, which needs 間 without に. 間に is for something that happens at one point inside the period.
mistake.right: 電車を待っている間、ずっと本を読んでいました。

distinguish_from.note: ながら is one person doing two things at once. 間 and 間に mark a period, and the two parts can have different subjects.

entries.title: Making something (a certain way)
entries.meaning: い-adj (く) or な-adj / noun (に) + する: make something that way; someone deliberately causes the change.
entries.when: Use it when someone changes something on purpose: 部屋をきれいにする, "tidy the room"; 音を小さくする, "turn the sound down"; 髪を短くする. It is common in requests: 静かにしてください, "please be quiet".
entries.why: く and に are the forms adjectives take to describe how. する is "do, make". So 小さくする is "make (it) so that it is small". It is the transitive partner of くなる／になる: なる says a change happens (音が小さくなる), する says someone makes it happen (音を小さくする). That is why the thing changed takes を, and why requests to change something use する.

formation.form: Noun を + い-adjective (drop い) + く + する
formation.note: 小さくする, 短くする, 安くする; いい → よくする.

formation.form: Noun を + な-adjective / noun + に + する
formation.note: きれいにする, 静かにする, 半分にする.

examples.japanese: テレビの音を小さくしてください。
examples.reading: テレビのおとをちいさくしてください。
examples.romaji: terebi no oto o chiisaku shite kudasai.
examples.english: Please turn the TV down.

examples.japanese: 週末に部屋をきれいにしました。
examples.reading: しゅうまつにへやをきれいにしました。
examples.romaji: shūmatsu ni heya o kirei ni shimashita.
examples.english: I tidied my room at the weekend.

examples.japanese: 髪を短くしました。
examples.reading: かみをみじかくしました。
examples.romaji: kami o mijikaku shimashita.
examples.english: I got my hair cut short.

examples.japanese: 図書館では静かにしてください。
examples.reading: としょかんではしずかにしてください。
examples.romaji: toshokan de wa shizuka ni shite kudasai.
examples.english: Please be quiet in the library.

mistake.wrong: 部屋がきれいにしました。
mistake.problem: する says someone makes the change, so the thing changed is the object and takes を. が goes with なる (部屋がきれいになりました).
mistake.right: 部屋をきれいにしました。

distinguish_from.note: くなる／になる says a change happens by itself (が). くする／にする says someone causes it (を).
Noun + にする on its own is "decide on, choose" (コーヒーにします). Here にする after an adjective means "make it so".

entries.title: Even though (and that's not how it should be)
entries.meaning: Plain form + のに: "even though A, B"; B goes against what A led you to expect, often with surprise or frustration.
entries.when: Use it when a result goes against what the first fact would lead you to expect, and you feel something about it: disappointment, surprise, complaint. 一生懸命勉強したのに、試験に落ちました, "even though I studied hard, I failed the exam". Both parts are real facts. Left at the end of a sentence, it sighs: もっと早く言えばよかったのに, "you should have told me sooner".
entries.why: の turns A into a fact, and に sets it against B: "given the fact A, still B". Because A is a fact, のに is not used for "even if" about something that may happen; that is ても. Because the speaker is reacting to a result, B is not a request, an invitation or the speaker's own plan. A noun or な-adjective takes な before のに (日曜日なのに, 静かなのに), as with other の-patterns.

formation.note: 勉強したのに, 来ないのに, 安いのに.

formation.form: Noun / な-adjective + な + のに
formation.note: 日曜日なのに, 静かなのに.

examples.japanese: 一生懸命勉強したのに、試験に落ちました。
examples.reading: いっしょうけんめいべんきょうしたのに、しけんにおちました。
examples.romaji: isshōkenmei benkyō shita noni, shiken ni ochimashita.
examples.english: Even though I studied hard, I failed the exam.

examples.japanese: 日曜日なのに、会社に行かなければなりません。
examples.reading: にちようびなのに、かいしゃにいかなければなりません。
examples.romaji: nichiyōbi na noni, kaisha ni ikanakereba narimasen.
examples.english: Even though it's Sunday, I have to go to work.

examples.japanese: 約束したのに、彼は来ませんでした。
examples.reading: やくそくしたのに、かれはきませんでした。
examples.romaji: yakusoku shita noni, kare wa kimasen deshita.
examples.english: He promised, and yet he didn't come.

mistake.wrong: 明日雨が降るのに、サッカーをします。
mistake.problem: Meant as "even if it rains tomorrow". のに is for facts that already hold; for "even if" about what may happen, use ても.
mistake.right: 明日雨が降っても、サッカーをします。

distinguish_from.note: ても covers "even if" for things that may happen, and is neutral. のに is for facts, and carries the speaker's reaction.
が and けど simply join two contrasting facts. のに adds that the result is unexpected or unwelcome.

review.note: Covers the "even though" のに only. The purpose のに (この箱は本を入れるのに使います, "used for holding books") is a different point and is not written here.

entries.title: Like, such as (before a noun)
entries.meaning: N のような + noun: "a (noun) like N"; compares, or gives N as an example of the kind meant.
entries.when: Use it before a noun to compare (夢のような一日, "a day like a dream") or to give an example of the kind of thing you mean (ラーメンのような温かい物, "something warm, like ramen"). In conversation, みたいな is common: 東京みたいな町.
entries.why: よう means "manner, likeness". The noun joins it with の, and ような then joins the next noun with な, the way a な-adjective does. So N のような X is "an X of N's kind". Whether that compares X to N or offers N as an example comes from the context. The form before a verb or adjective is ように (OJG-0088): the choice depends on what comes next.

formation.form: Noun + の + ような + noun
formation.note: 夢のような一日, 父のような人.
夢を見ているような気持ち, "a feeling as if I were dreaming".

examples.japanese: 父のような優しい人になりたいです。
examples.reading: ちちのようなやさしいひとになりたいです。
examples.romaji: chichi no yō na yasashii hito ni naritai desu.
examples.english: I want to become a kind person like my father.

examples.japanese: ラーメンのような温かい物が食べたいです。
examples.reading: ラーメンのようなあたたかいものがたべたいです。
examples.romaji: rāmen no yō na atatakai mono ga tabetai desu.
examples.english: I want to eat something warm, like ramen.

examples.japanese: 夢のような一日でした。
examples.reading: ゆめのようないちにちでした。
examples.romaji: yume no yō na ichinichi deshita.
examples.english: It was a day like a dream.

mistake.wrong: 父ような人になりたいです。
mistake.problem: After a noun, よう needs の.
mistake.right: 父のような人になりたいです。

distinguish_from.note: ように goes before a verb or adjective (魚のように泳ぐ). ような goes before a noun.
みたいな is the conversational equivalent and joins the noun directly, without の.

entries.title: Like, as (before a verb or adjective)
entries.meaning: N のように + verb or adjective: "like N", "as N does"; also "as" in 次のように, 言ったように.
entries.when: Use it to say how something is done or how something is, by comparison: 魚のように泳ぐ, "swim like a fish"; 春のように暖かい, "as warm as spring". It also means "as" when pointing to something shown or said: 次のように書いてください, "write it as follows"; 前にも言ったように, "as I said before".
entries.why: のように is the adverb form of のような. Like a な-adjective (静かな部屋, 静かに話す), it takes な before a noun and に before a verb or adjective. So choose by what comes next. With a verb before it (言ったように), it points to the way something was said or shown: "in the way that…".

formation.form: Noun + の + ように + verb or adjective
formation.note: 魚のように泳ぐ, 春のように暖かい. Conversation: みたいに.
言ったように, 次に書いてあるように.

examples.japanese: マリアさんは日本人のように日本語を話します。
examples.reading: マリアさんはにほんじんのようににほんごをはなします。
examples.romaji: maria-san wa nihonjin no yō ni nihongo o hanashimasu.
examples.english: Maria speaks Japanese like a native speaker.

examples.japanese: 今日は春のように暖かいです。
examples.reading: きょうははるのようにあたたかいです。
examples.romaji: kyō wa haru no yō ni atatakai desu.
examples.english: Today is as warm as spring.

examples.japanese: 次のように書いてください。
examples.reading: つぎのようにかいてください。
examples.romaji: tsugi no yō ni kaite kudasai.
examples.english: Please write it as follows.

mistake.wrong: 魚のような泳ぎます。
mistake.problem: Before a verb, the adverb form ように is needed. ような goes only before a noun.
mistake.right: 魚のように泳ぎます。

distinguish_from.note: ような goes before a noun. ように goes before a verb or adjective.
The ように of ように言う follows a verb and reports an instruction. This ように compares or points to a manner.

entries.title: Being made to do something (the causative passive)
entries.meaning: Causative passive V-させられる: "be made to V", usually against your will; the one made to act is the subject.
entries.when: Use it to say, from your own side, that someone made you do something you did not want to do: 子どものころ、母に野菜を食べさせられました, "as a child, my mother made me eat vegetables". The one who made you is marked with に. Being kept waiting is a common case: 一時間も待たされました.
entries.why: It stacks two changes. The causative (食べさせる) adds someone who makes another act. The passive (られる) then turns the one who acted into the subject, and moves the causer to に. So the sentence is about the person who had to act, and like other passives it usually carries a sense of being put upon. Godan verbs have a shorter spoken form, される for せられる (飲まされる, 待たされる), except those ending in す (話させられる).

formation.note: 食べる → 食べさせられる.

formation.form: Godan verb (ない-stem) + せられる, or される
formation.note: 飲む → 飲ませられる／飲まされる, 待つ → 待たされる. Verbs in す take only させられる (話させられる).

formation.form: する → させられる; 来る → 来させられる (こさせられる)

examples.japanese: 子どものころ、母に野菜を食べさせられました。
examples.reading: こどものころ、ははにやさいをたべさせられました。
examples.romaji: kodomo no koro, haha ni yasai o tabesaseraremashita.
examples.english: When I was a child, my mother made me eat vegetables.

examples.japanese: 駅で一時間も待たされました。
examples.reading: えきでいちじかんもまたされました。
examples.romaji: eki de ichijikan mo matasaremashita.
examples.english: I was kept waiting at the station for a whole hour.

examples.japanese: 先輩にお酒をたくさん飲まされました。
examples.reading: せんぱいにおさけをたくさんのまされました。
examples.romaji: senpai ni osake o takusan nomasaremashita.
examples.english: My senior made me drink a lot.

mistake.wrong: 母は私に野菜を食べさせられました。
mistake.problem: The roles are reversed. In the causative passive, the one who was made to act is the subject, and the one who made them takes に.
mistake.right: 私は母に野菜を食べさせられました。

distinguish_from.note: させる tells it from the causer's side (母が私に食べさせた). させられる tells it from the side of the one made to act.
られる is "have something done to you". させられる is "be made to do something yourself".

entries.title: Deciding to do something
entries.meaning: V (plain) + ことにする: "decide to V", by one's own choice; ことにしている: "make a point of V-ing".
entries.when: Use it to say you, or someone, decided on an action: 来年、日本に留学することにしました, "I've decided to study in Japan next year". With a negative verb, decide not to: 甘い物を食べないことにした. ことにしている describes a personal rule you keep: 毎朝走ることにしています.
entries.why: こと turns the verb into a noun, "doing V", and にする is "settle on", the same にする as in コーヒーにします, "I'll have coffee". So ことにする is "settle on doing V". It is a decision made by the person, in contrast to ことになる, where the matter is decided by others or by circumstances. The past, ことにした, is the usual way to announce a decision just made, and ことにしている says the decision is still being kept.

formation.form: V (dictionary form or ない-form) + ことにする
formation.note: 留学することにした, 食べないことにした.
A rule or habit you have set yourself.

examples.japanese: 来年、日本に留学することにしました。
examples.reading: らいねん、にほんにりゅうがくすることにしました。
examples.romaji: rainen, nihon ni ryūgaku suru koto ni shimashita.
examples.english: I've decided to study abroad in Japan next year.

examples.japanese: 今日から甘い物を食べないことにします。
examples.reading: きょうからあまいものをたべないことにします。
examples.romaji: kyō kara amai mono o tabenai koto ni shimasu.
examples.english: From today, I'm not going to eat sweets.

examples.japanese: 毎朝三十分走ることにしています。
examples.reading: まいあささんじゅっぷんはしることにしています。
examples.romaji: maiasa sanjuppun hashiru koto ni shite imasu.
examples.english: I make a point of running for thirty minutes every morning.

mistake.wrong: 父の仕事で、来年アメリカに引っ越すことにしました。
mistake.problem: The move is decided by the father's job, not by the speaker. For something decided by others or by circumstances, use ことになる.
mistake.right: 父の仕事で、来年アメリカに引っ越すことになりました。

distinguish_from.note: ことになる is decided by others or by circumstances. ことにする is your own decision.
つもり is an intention you hold. ことにした announces the moment of deciding.

listed.item: 文A。だから 文B (Bun A. Dakara Bun B)

entries.title: And so, that's why
entries.meaning: それで: "and so", "that's why"; starts a sentence that gives the result of what was just said. Also "and then?".
entries.when: Use it at the start of a sentence to give what followed from the previous one: 昨日は熱がありました。それで、学校を休みました, "I had a fever yesterday. So I stayed home from school". In conversation, それで？ asks the other person to go on: "and then?".
entries.why: それ points back at the previous sentence, and で presents it as the cause: "with that, …". So the second sentence is what came about because of the first. Because it reports a result, it is used for things that happened or hold, and not to lead into your own request, suggestion or order; だから is used for those.

examples.japanese: 昨日は熱がありました。それで、学校を休みました。
examples.reading: きのうはねつがありました。それで、がっこうをやすみました。
examples.romaji: kinō wa netsu ga arimashita. sorede, gakkō o yasumimashita.
examples.english: I had a fever yesterday. So I stayed home from school.

examples.japanese: 電車が遅れました。それで、会議に間に合いませんでした。
examples.reading: でんしゃがおくれました。それで、かいぎにまにあいませんでした。
examples.romaji: densha ga okuremashita. sorede, kaigi ni maniaimasen deshita.
examples.english: The train was late. That's why I didn't make it to the meeting.

examples.japanese: 「駅で田中さんに会ったんです。」「それで？」
examples.reading: 「えきでたなかさんにあったんです。」「それで？」
examples.romaji: "eki de tanaka-san ni atta n desu." "sorede?"
examples.english: "I ran into Tanaka-san at the station." "And then?"

mistake.wrong: 明日はテストがあります。それで、今日は早く寝てください。
mistake.problem: それで introduces a result that came about. It does not lead into a request; use だから.
mistake.right: 明日はテストがあります。だから、今日は早く寝てください。

distinguish_from.note: だから can lead into anything, including requests and opinions. それで reports a result.

listed.item: 文A。それで 文B (Bun A. Sorede Bun B)

entries.title: Besides, what's more
entries.meaning: それに／そのうえ: "besides", "on top of that"; adds another point of the same kind to what was just said.
entries.when: Use it at the start of a sentence to add a further point pushing in the same direction: この店は安いです。それに、料理もおいしいです. それに is common in conversation; そのうえ is a little more formal and suggests "and even more than that". Both often add one more reason.
entries.why: それ points back at what was said, and に adds to it: "to that, (add) this". そのうえ is literally "on top of that". Both pile points up, so the added point goes the same way as the first: good on good, or bad on bad. To add a point that goes against the first, use でも or しかし.

examples.japanese: この店は安いです。それに、料理もおいしいです。
examples.reading: このみせはやすいです。それに、りょうりもおいしいです。
examples.romaji: kono mise wa yasui desu. soreni, ryōri mo oishii desu.
examples.english: This restaurant is cheap. Besides, the food is good too.

examples.japanese: 今日は雨です。それに、とても寒いです。
examples.reading: きょうはあめです。それに、とてもさむいです。
examples.romaji: kyō wa ame desu. soreni, totemo samui desu.
examples.english: It's raining today. And on top of that, it's very cold.

examples.japanese: 道に迷いました。そのうえ、スマホの電池も切れてしまいました。
examples.reading: みちにまよいました。そのうえ、スマホのでんちもきれてしまいました。
examples.romaji: michi ni mayoimashita. sono ue, sumaho no denchi mo kirete shimaimashita.
examples.english: I got lost. On top of that, my phone battery ran out.

mistake.wrong: このアパートは駅から近いです。それに、家賃が高いです。
mistake.problem: それに adds a point of the same kind, but "close to the station" is good and "the rent is high" is bad. For a point that goes against the first, use でも.
mistake.right: このアパートは駅から近いです。でも、家賃が高いです。

distinguish_from.note: そして and それから add the next thing, or what happened next, with no weighing. それに piles up another point for the same conclusion.
し piles up points inside one sentence. それに starts a new sentence to add one.

Aと Bと どちら～ (A to B to dochira~)
AとBと どっち〜 (A to B to docchi〜)
A は B が〜 (A wa B ga〜)

entries.title: A is not as … as B
entries.meaning: A は B ほど + negative: "A is not as (adjective) as B"; B sets a level that A does not reach.
entries.when: Use it to compare by saying one thing falls short of another: 今年の夏は去年ほど暑くない, "this summer isn't as hot as last year's". It is a natural way to say something is less so, and it sounds gentler than a direct comparison with より.
entries.why: ほど means "extent, degree". B ほど is "to B's degree", and the negative says A does not reach it. So the end of the sentence must be negative; A は B ほど暑い is not a comparison. The sentence also takes for granted that B has the quality to a clear degree: 去年ほど暑くない implies last year was hot.

formation.form: A は B ほど + negative
formation.note: い-adjective 暑くない; な-adjective にぎやかではない／じゃない; verb 読まない. Polite くないです／くありません, ではありません, ません.

examples.reading: ことしのなつはきょねんほどあつくないです。
examples.romaji: kotoshi no natsu wa kyonen hodo atsuku nai desu.
examples.english: This summer isn't as hot as last year's.

examples.japanese: 私の町は東京ほどにぎやかではありません。
examples.reading: わたしのまちはとうきょうほどにぎやかではありません。
examples.romaji: watashi no machi wa tōkyō hodo nigiyaka de wa arimasen.
examples.english: My town isn't as lively as Tokyo.

examples.japanese: 弟は私ほど本を読みません。
examples.reading: おとうとはわたしほどほんをよみません。
examples.romaji: otōto wa watashi hodo hon o yomimasen.
examples.english: My little brother doesn't read as much as I do.

mistake.wrong: 東京は大阪ほど大きいです。
mistake.problem: ほど in a comparison needs a negative. To say A is bigger than B, use より.
mistake.right: 東京は大阪より大きいです。

distinguish_from.note: より and のほうが say which one has more of the quality. ほど～ない says one falls short of the other.

entries.title: By (a deadline)
entries.meaning: Time + までに: "by (then)", "before (then)"; a one-time action happens at some point before the deadline.
entries.when: Use it for a deadline: 金曜日までにレポートを出してください, "please hand in the report by Friday". The action is done once, at any point up to that time. It can also follow a verb: 暗くなるまでに帰ります, "I'll be home before it gets dark".
entries.why: まで is "until" and marks the end of a stretch of time; に marks a point where something happens. Together they say "at some point within the stretch up to X". That is why までに goes with one-time actions (出す, 帰る, 着く, 終わる). まで without に says an action lasts all the way to X (五時まで働く), so its verb is one that goes on.

formation.note: 金曜日までに, 三時までに.
暗くなるまでに, 母が帰るまでに.

examples.japanese: 金曜日までにレポートを出してください。
examples.reading: きんようびまでにレポートをだしてください。
examples.romaji: kin'yōbi made ni repōto o dashite kudasai.
examples.english: Please hand in the report by Friday.

examples.japanese: 暗くなるまでに帰ります。
examples.reading: くらくなるまでにかえります。
examples.romaji: kuraku naru made ni kaerimasu.
examples.english: I'll be home before it gets dark.

examples.japanese: 三時までに駅に来てください。
examples.reading: さんじまでにえきにきてください。
examples.romaji: sanji made ni eki ni kite kudasai.
examples.english: Please come to the station by three.

mistake.wrong: 五時までに働きます。
mistake.problem: 働く goes on over time, and the speaker means it lasts until five. That is まで. までに is for a one-time action done before a deadline.
mistake.right: 五時まで働きます。

distinguish_from.note: まで marks how long something goes on ("until"). までに marks a deadline for a one-time action ("by").

entries.title: Not that (much), not so
entries.meaning: そんなに + negative: "not that (adjective)", "not so much"; tones down a degree the listener might expect.
entries.when: Use it to say something is less than might be thought: この料理はそんなに辛くないですよ, "this dish isn't that spicy". It is common in modest or reassuring answers: 「日本語が上手ですね。」「いいえ、そんなに上手じゃないです。」. Without a negative, そんなに means "that much", usually with surprise: そんなに食べたの？
entries.why: そんな points at something near the listener or already mentioned: "that kind, to that degree". So そんなに～ない says "not to the degree you have in mind", measured against what the listener said or might expect. That is why it sits naturally in answers and reassurances. あまり～ない is a general "not very"; そんなに ties the degree to what was said or expected.

formation.note: い-adjective 辛くない; な-adjective 上手じゃない; verb 食べない.

entries.pattern: さしあげる／いただく／くださる
entries.title: Giving and receiving with respect
entries.meaning: さしあげる (give, humble), いただく (receive, humble), くださる (give me, honorific): あげる, もらう, くれる towards superiors.
entries.when: Use them in place of あげる, もらう and くれる when the other person is someone you show respect to, such as a teacher, a customer or someone older: 先生に辞書をいただきました, "I received a dictionary from my teacher"; 社長がお土産をくださいました, "the company president gave me a souvenir".
entries.why: Each keeps the direction of its plain verb and adds respect. さしあげる and いただく are humble: they lower your own side, whether you are the giver or the receiver. くださる is honorific: it raises the superior who gives to you. So your own action takes the humble verb, and the superior's action takes the honorific one. くださる has an irregular ます-form, くださいます. いただく is also the humble verb for eating and drinking, as in いただきます.

formation.note: Humble あげる. You or your side give to a superior.
Humble もらう. You receive from a superior, marked with に or から.
Honorific くれる. A superior gives to you. Polite: くださいます, くださいました.

entries.pattern: ～てさしあげる／～ていただく／～てくださる
entries.title: Doing favours with respect
entries.meaning: V-てさしあげる, V-ていただく, V-てくださる: てあげる, てもらう, てくれる when a superior gives or receives the favour.
entries.when: Use ていただく and てくださる when someone above you does something for you: 先生に作文を直していただきました and 先生が作文を直してくださいました both mean the teacher corrected your essay, the first told from your side, the second from the teacher's. てさしあげる is for doing a favour for a superior, and is used with care.
entries.why: These are the respectful favour verbs, with the same directions as the plain ones. ていただく, the humble もらう, keeps you as the subject and marks the superior with に. てくださる, the honorific くれる, makes the superior the subject. ていただく is very common in polite speech, because it lets you acknowledge a kindness while humbly staying the subject. てさしあげる still announces that you did someone a favour, so to that person's face it can sound presumptuous, and speakers often choose another humble expression instead.

formation.note: The superior is marked with に. Polite いただきます.
The superior is the subject. Polite くださいます.
You do something for a superior. Used with care.

entries.pattern: ～てくれませんか／～てもらえませんか／～てくださいませんか
entries.title: Would you…? Could you…? (polite requests)
entries.meaning: V-てくれませんか, V-てもらえませんか, V-てくださいませんか: polite requests, softer than てください.
entries.when: Use them to ask someone to do something politely: ちょっと手伝ってくれませんか, "could you give me a hand?". てくれませんか suits people you are on polite but familiar terms with; てもらえませんか is a little more modest; てくださいませんか is more polite, for superiors and strangers. The most polite everyday form is ていただけませんか (OJG-0058). Casual: てくれない？, てもらえない？
entries.why: てください is polite, but it is still an instruction. These forms turn it into a negative question, which leaves the listener room to say no and so sounds softer. With くれる and くださる you ask "won't you give me V-ing?", with the listener as the one acting. もらえる is the potential form of もらう, so てもらえませんか asks "can't I receive V-ing?", from your own side. Asking about your receiving is less direct than asking the listener to act, which is why it feels more modest.

formation.form: V (て-form) + もらえませんか
formation.note: The potential form もらえる, "can receive".

formation.form: V (て-form) + くださいませんか
formation.note: てくれますか, てもらえますか and てくださいますか also occur and are a little more direct.

entries.title: Wanting someone to do something
entries.meaning: V-てほしい: "I want (someone) to V"; a wish about another person's action. Negative: ないでほしい.
entries.when: Use it to say what you want someone else to do: 母に早く元気になってほしい, "I want my mother to get well soon". The person is marked with に. Negative: 行かないでほしい, "I don't want you to go". Said to someone, it works as an indirect request; towards a superior, ていただきたい is used instead.
entries.why: ほしい is "want (a thing)". After a て-form, the thing wanted is another person's action. Because ほしい is your own feeling, the one who wants is the speaker, or the listener in a question, and the one who should act is someone else, marked with に as the person you want it from. たい cannot do this job: it is only for your own actions.

formation.note: Polite: ほしいです; softened: ほしいんですが.

formation.form: (person に) V (ない-form) + でほしい

entries.pattern: ～てもらいたい／～ていただきたい
entries.title: I'd like (someone) to do…
entries.meaning: V-てもらいたい, V-ていただきたい (humble): "I'd like (someone) to V"; a wish, or a firm request, about someone's action.
entries.when: Use it to say you want someone to do something for you, often as a polite but firm request: この書類を明日までに出していただきたいんですが. ていただきたい is the humble form, for superiors and customers; てもらいたい is for equals and people below you. Adding んですが or けど softens it.
entries.why: たい added to もらう, "receive", gives "want to receive". So てもらいたい is "want to receive V-ing from someone": the wish is about your own receiving, which is why たい can be used even though someone else acts. The one who acts is marked with に, as with てもらう. It means about the same as てほしい, but because it is built on a receiving verb, it has a humble form, ていただきたい, for polite situations. It still states your wish directly, so it can sound demanding without a softener.

entries.title: I think (that)…
entries.meaning: Plain form + と思う: "I think (that)…"; presents a statement as the speaker's opinion or guess.
entries.when: Use it to give your opinion or a guess: 明日は雨が降ると思います, "I think it will rain tomorrow"; この映画はおもしろいと思います. For what someone else thinks, use と思っている: 兄は日本語は難しいと思っています. Japanese speakers also use it to soften statements.
entries.why: と marks what is thought, like quotation marks, and 思う is "think". So the part before と is a complete statement in plain form, with its own tense and negation, and a noun or な-adjective needs だ to make it complete (先生だと思う). 思う reports an inner process, so a plain と思う is the speaker's own thought (or the listener's, in a question); another person's opinion is reported with と思っている. For a negative opinion, Japanese usually makes the content negative: 来ないと思う, "I don't think he'll come".

formation.form: Verb / い-adjective (plain form) + と思う

formation.form: Noun / な-adjective + だ + と思う

entries.pattern: ～なければならない／～なくてはいけない／～ないといけない
entries.title: Must, have to
entries.meaning: V-なければならない／V-なくてはいけない／V-ないといけない: "must V", "have to V".
entries.when: Use these to say something is necessary: 明日は六時に起きなければなりません, "I have to get up at six tomorrow". なければならない is the most formal and the usual choice in writing; ないといけない and なくてはいけない are common in speech. In casual speech they shrink to なきゃ and なくちゃ (OJG-0037).
entries.why: All three say "if you don't V, it won't do". The first half (なければ, なくては, ないと) sets up "not doing V", and ならない or いけない says that is not acceptable. Two negatives make "must". ならない tends to sound like a general or objective necessity, and いけない more like a personal or situational one, but in everyday speech they overlap a great deal. All are built on the ない-form: 行かない → 行かなければ, 行かなくては, 行かないと.

formation.form: V (ない-form, drop い) + ければならない
formation.note: 起きなければならない. Polite なりません.

formation.form: V (ない-form, drop い) + くてはいけない

entries.title: Things like A and B (examples, in conversation)
entries.meaning: A とか B (とか): "things like A and B", "A, B and so on"; gives examples from a larger set. Conversational.
entries.when: Use it in conversation to give a few examples: 休みの日は、映画とか買い物とかに行きます, "on days off I go to films, go shopping and so on". Unlike や, it can join verbs and whole clauses: 掃除するとか、洗濯するとか. A single とか makes a suggestion vague and gentle: お茶とか飲みませんか, "how about some tea or something?".
entries.why: とか is built from と, which quotes, and か, which marks uncertainty: "things such as…, or something". So it names examples without claiming the list is complete, like や, but more loosely: it can follow nouns, verbs and clauses, and a single とか leaves the suggestion open. Because it is loose and conversational, や (with など) is the usual choice for listing nouns in writing and formal speech.

formation.note: The second とか is often kept before a particle (映画とか買い物とかに), and may be dropped.

formation.form: Verb (plain form) とか verb とか
formation.note: 掃除するとか、洗濯するとか.

entries.title: In the middle of (an activity)
entries.meaning: Noun + 中 (ちゅう): "in the middle of N", "now doing N", as in 会議中, "in a meeting", or 工事中, "under construction".
entries.when: Use it after a noun that names an activity to say it is going on now: 会議中, "in a meeting"; 電話中, "on the phone"; 授業中, "during class"; 工事中, "under construction". It is very common on signs and in short statements: 田中は今、会議中です.
entries.why: 中 means "middle, inside". After a noun of activity, read ちゅう, it says someone or something is inside that activity, partway through it. It works with nouns, most often Sino-Japanese nouns for activities (会議, 食事, 勉強, 工事), and the result is itself a noun, used with です or with の before another noun (授業中の教室). It is not added to verbs; for "in the middle of doing" with a verb, use ているところ. The same kanji read じゅう after a period or a place means "throughout" (一日中, "all day"; 世界中, "all over the world"), which is a different use.

formation.note: 会議中, 電話中, 食事中, 工事中, 営業中. Used with です, or with の before a noun.

mistake.problem: 中 follows a noun of activity, not a verb. Use the noun 食事, or a verb with ているところ.

entries.title: About to, in the middle of, just done
entries.meaning: V + ところ: a stage of an action; about to (V-るところ), in the middle of (V-ているところ), or just done (V-たところ).
entries.when: Use it to say exactly where you are in an action: 今から出かけるところです, "I'm just about to go out"; 今、晩ご飯を作っているところです, "I'm in the middle of making dinner"; 今、駅に着いたところです, "I've just got to the station". It is common when explaining why you cannot do something right now.
entries.why: ところ means "place", here a place in time: a point in the course of an action. The verb form before it chooses the point: the dictionary form looks ahead (about to), ている is inside the action (in the middle of it), and た is just after it (just done). ところ is a noun, so it is followed by です or だ. たところ is about the moment right after an action, so it goes with 今 or さっき, not with something long ago.

In the middle of.

mistake.problem: たところ is for the moment just after an action, and last year is not that. For something that feels recent from the speaker's point of view, use たばかり.
mistake.right: 去年日本に来たばかりです。

distinguish_from.note: たばかり says something happened recently, as the speaker feels it, and can reach back months. たところ is the moment right after.
Noun + 中 says "in the middle of" with a noun (食事中). ているところ says it with a verb.

Verb て いる ところ (Verb te iru tokoro)

entries.title: Going and coming, in space and in time
entries.meaning: V-ていく／V-てくる: do V and go / come; also change moving on from now (ていく) or up to now (てくる).
entries.when: Use them first for movement: 傘を持っていく, "take an umbrella (with you)"; パンを買ってくる, "go and buy bread (and come back)". Then for change over time: これからもっと寒くなっていく, "it will keep getting colder"; 日本語がわかってきた, "I've begun to understand Japanese". てくる also marks something starting to come towards you: 雨が降ってきた, "it's started to rain".
entries.why: いく and くる are "go" and "come", pointing away from the speaker and towards the speaker. After the て-form, they add that direction to the action. In space, 持っていく is "hold it and go (away)" and 持ってくる is "hold it and come (here)". The same picture works for time, with "now" as where the speaker stands: ていく is change going forward from now, and てくる is change that has come up to now, or is just beginning to show. As helpers, いく and くる are usually written in kana.

formation.note: Polite: ていきます. Casual: てく (持ってく).

entries.title: Sometimes; there are times when
entries.meaning: V (dictionary or ない-form) + ことがある: "sometimes V", "there are times when (I don't) V".
entries.when: Use it for something that happens now and then, not regularly: 忙しいときは、朝ご飯を食べないことがあります, "when I'm busy, I sometimes skip breakfast"; この電車はときどき遅れることがあります. Do not confuse it with たことがある, which is about experience.
entries.why: こと turns the verb into a noun, "the case of V-ing", and がある says such cases exist. With a non-past verb, "there are occasions when V" means "sometimes". With a past verb, たことがある, the thing that exists is a past event, so it means "have done it before". The verb form decides the meaning. It often comes with ときどき or たまに.

formation.note: 遅れることがある. Polite ことがあります.
食べないことがある, "sometimes I don't eat".

entries.title: I'm thinking of doing…
entries.meaning: Volitional + と思う: "I'm thinking of V-ing", "I intend to V"; an intention the speaker has formed.
entries.when: Use it to tell someone what you intend to do: 夏休みに国へ帰ろうと思います, "I'm thinking of going home for the summer holidays". と思っている suggests an intention you have held for some time: 来年、日本語の試験を受けようと思っています.
entries.why: The volitional form (帰ろう) is the speaker's will, "I'll go home", and と思う frames it as a thought: "I think, 'I'll go home'". So it reports an intention instead of declaring a decision on the spot, which sounds gentler than a bare statement. と思っている stretches the thought over time, as an intention that has been held for a while, and can also report someone else's intention: 兄は車を買おうと思っています.

formation.note: 帰ろうと思う, 受けようと思う, しようと思う.
An intention held for some time, or someone else's.

mistake.problem: Meant as an intention. The dictionary form + と思う is a prediction, "I think I'll (probably) go home". For your own intention, use the volitional form.

distinguish_from.note: The volitional form on its own declares a decision or invites. With と思う it reports an intention.
つもり is a firm plan. ようと思う is an intention you are thinking about, often less settled.

listed.item: Verb ようと思う (Verb-you to omou)

entries.title: Tell someone to do something (reported)
entries.meaning: V (dictionary or ない-form) + ように言う: "tell (someone) to V / not to V"; reports an instruction or request.
entries.when: Use it to report what someone told someone to do: 先生は学生に、宿題を出すように言いました, "the teacher told the students to hand in their homework". With a negative verb: "not to". Other verbs of passing on work the same way: ように頼む, "ask to"; ように伝える, "pass on (the message) to".
entries.why: ように is "so that, in such a way that": the verb before it is the aim. ように言う is "say, so that someone will V", the content of an instruction reported in plain form instead of quoted. It passes the instruction on without its exact words or politeness: 出してください becomes 出すように. The person told is marked with に. To quote the exact words, use 「…てください」と言いました.

formation.form: (person に) V (dictionary form) + ように言う
formation.note: 出すように言った. Also ように頼む, ように伝える.

formation.form: (person に) V (ない-form) + ように言う
formation.note: 飲まないように言った. Passive, "was told to": ように言われた.

entries.title: Suddenly start to
entries.meaning: V (ます-stem) + 出す: "start to V", usually suddenly or unexpectedly; in some compounds, literally "out".
entries.when: Use it for an action or event that starts suddenly or without warning: 急に雨が降り出しました, "it suddenly started to rain"; 赤ちゃんが泣き出しました, "the baby burst into tears". In some compound verbs 出す keeps its meaning "out": 取り出す, "take out"; 思い出す, "recall".
entries.why: 出す means "put out, let out". Joined to a ます-stem, it presents the action as breaking out into the open, which is why starts made with 出す often feel sudden or beyond anyone's control: 泣き出す, 笑い出す, 降り出す. It is not the verb for a planned start, such as starting a study plan; that is 始める. The compound is a godan verb (降り出す, 降り出した).

formation.note: 降り出す, 泣き出す, 走り出す, 笑い出す.

entries.title: Finish doing
entries.meaning: V (ます-stem) + 終わる: "finish V-ing"; the action is carried through to its end.
entries.when: Use it to say an action has been completed: やっと本を読み終わりました, "I've finally finished reading the book"; 食べ終わったら、お皿を洗ってください. It fits actions with a natural end: reading a book, eating a meal, writing a report.
entries.why: 終わる means "come to an end". Joined to a ます-stem, it says the action reached its end: 読み終わる is "read to the end". Because there has to be an end to reach, it goes with actions that have one (a book, a meal, a letter), and not with open-ended ones such as 待つ. The object of the first verb keeps を: 本を読み終わる. In writing, 終える is also used (読み終える).

formation.note: 読み終わる, 食べ終わる, 書き終わる. Written style also 終える.

distinguish_from.note: 続ける says the action keeps going. 終わる says it reached its end.
てしまう can also mean "finish completely", but often adds regret. 終わる simply reports the end.

entries.title: Keep on doing
entries.meaning: V (ます-stem) + 続ける: "keep V-ing", "continue to V"; the action goes on without stopping.
entries.when: Use it for an action that goes on, often longer than expected or in spite of something: 三時間歩き続けました, "I kept walking for three hours". For things that happen by themselves, such as rain, 続く is also used: 雨が降り続いています.
entries.why: 続ける is "continue (something)". Joined to a ます-stem, it says the action keeps going. It is an ichidan verb (続けます, 続けて). Because it is about going on, it fits actions that can last or repeat (歩く, 待つ, 話す), not one-moment ones such as 着く. With natural events, where nobody is doing the continuing, the intransitive 続く is common: 降り続く. For a する-verb, the stem is し: 勉強し続ける.

formation.note: 歩き続ける, 待ち続ける, 話し続ける, 勉強し続ける.
For natural events such as rain (降り続く).

ている says an action is under way. 続ける stresses that it goes on and on.

listed.item: Verb + 続ける (つづける, tsuzukeru)

entries.title: How to do, the way of doing
entries.meaning: V (ます-stem) + 方 (かた): "the way of V-ing", "how to V"; makes a noun.
entries.when: Use it to talk about how something is done: この漢字の読み方, "how to read this kanji"; この機械の使い方を教えてください, "please show me how to use this machine". Common ones are 作り方, "recipe, how to make"; 行き方, "how to get there"; and 書き方.
entries.why: 方, read かた, means "way, manner". Joined to a ます-stem, it makes a noun: 読み方 is "way of reading". Because the result is a noun, the verb's を-object cannot stay with を; it joins the noun with の instead: 漢字を読む → 漢字の読み方. Other particles are kept and take の: 駅までの行き方. For a する-verb, し + 方 is 仕方 (しかた): 勉強の仕方. The same kanji read ほう is a different word, "side, direction", as in ほうがいい.

formation.note: The を-object becomes Noun + の. Other particles add の (までの, への).
For する-verbs: 勉強の仕方.

distinguish_from.note: 方 read ほう, as in ほうがいい, is a different word ("side, direction"). 方 read かた after a ます-stem is "way of doing".

entries.title: I wonder…
entries.meaning: Plain form + かな／かしら: "I wonder (if)…"; the speaker wonders aloud or to themselves. Casual.
entries.when: Use it when you wonder about something, half to yourself: 明日は晴れるかな, "I wonder if it'll be sunny tomorrow". It invites a response without asking directly. かな is used by everyone; かしら is traditionally women's speech and now sounds refined or a little old-fashioned. With a negative, it turns into a wish: バス、早く来ないかな, "I wish the bus would hurry up".
entries.why: か marks a question, and な (or しら) turns it inwards: instead of asking the listener, the speaker asks themselves. That is why it is softer than a question and fits talking to yourself. It is plain and casual, so in polite speech people use でしょうか, or wrap it: …かなと思います. A noun or な-adjective goes straight before it, without だ: 本当かな.

formation.form: Verb / い-adjective (plain form) + かな／かしら
formation.note: 晴れるかな, 開いているかな, おいしいかな.

formation.form: Noun / な-adjective + かな／かしら
formation.note: No だ: 本当かな, 誰かしら.
A wish that something would happen (早く来ないかな).

examples.japanese: 明日は晴れるかな。
examples.reading: あしたははれるかな。
examples.romaji: ashita wa hareru ka na.
examples.english: I wonder if it'll be sunny tomorrow.

examples.japanese: この店、まだ開いているかな。
examples.reading: このみせ、まだあいているかな。
examples.romaji: kono mise, mada aite iru ka na.
examples.english: I wonder if this shop is still open.

examples.japanese: バス、早く来ないかな。
examples.reading: バス、はやくこないかな。
examples.romaji: basu, hayaku konai ka na.
examples.english: I wish the bus would hurry up and come.

examples.japanese: あの人、誰かしら。
examples.reading: あのひと、だれかしら。
examples.romaji: ano hito, dare kashira.
examples.english: I wonder who that is.

mistake.wrong: お客様、こちらでよろしいかな。
mistake.problem: かな is casual, for talking to yourself or to friends. To a customer, ask politely with でしょうか.
mistake.right: お客様、こちらでよろしいでしょうか。

distinguish_from.note: でしょう guesses and でしょうか asks politely. かな wonders, casually and half to yourself.

entries.title: Please let me…
entries.meaning: Causative て-form + ください: "please let me V"; asks permission to do something yourself, often as a polite offer.
entries.when: Use it to ask to be allowed to do something: 少し考えさせてください, "please let me think about it for a while"; 今日は私に払わせてください, "please let me pay today". It is also a polite way to say what you would like to do: 明日は休ませてください. More polite: させていただけませんか.
entries.why: The causative (させる) is "make or let someone do", and てください asks the listener to do something. So させてください is "please let (me) do V": the listener is asked to be the one who allows, and the speaker is the one who acts. The speaker is usually left out, or marked with に (私に払わせてください). Because it asks permission, it sounds modest even when you are offering to do something for the listener. Casual: させて.

formation.note: 考えさせてください, 払わせてください, 休ませてください; する → させてください.

examples.japanese: 少し考えさせてください。
examples.reading: すこしかんがえさせてください。
examples.romaji: sukoshi kangaesasete kudasai.
examples.english: Please let me think about it for a while.

examples.japanese: 今日は私に払わせてください。
examples.reading: きょうはわたしにはらわせてください。
examples.romaji: kyō wa watashi ni harawasete kudasai.
examples.english: Please let me pay today.

examples.japanese: 明日は休ませてください。
examples.reading: あしたはやすませてください。
examples.romaji: ashita wa yasumasete kudasai.
examples.english: Please let me take tomorrow off.

mistake.wrong: 今日は私に払ってください。
mistake.problem: Meant as "let me pay". てください asks the listener to do the paying, so this says "please pay me". To ask to be allowed to pay yourself, use the causative.
mistake.right: 今日は私に払わせてください。

distinguish_from.note: させる is the causative in general. させてください uses it to ask permission for yourself.
てもいいですか asks whether something is allowed. させてください asks the listener to let you, and so leans more towards a request.

entries.title: Each, at a time
entries.meaning: Quantity + ずつ: "X each", "X at a time"; the same amount for each person, or in each step.
entries.when: Use it after a number or amount to say it is shared out equally or repeated in equal steps: 子どもたちにりんごを二つずつあげました, "I gave the children two apples each"; 毎日少しずつ, "a little at a time every day"; 一人ずつ入ってください, "please come in one at a time".
entries.why: ずつ follows a quantity and repeats it across units: for each person, each day, each turn, the same amount. That is why it follows numbers and words of amount (少し, 一つ, 一人, 半分), not ordinary nouns. 少しずつ, "little by little", is its most common use. Like other quantities, the phrase sits near the verb without a particle.

formation.note: 二つずつ, 一人ずつ, 一冊ずつ.
少しずつ, 半分ずつ.

examples.japanese: 子どもたちにりんごを二つずつあげました。
examples.reading: こどもたちにりんごをふたつずつあげました。
examples.romaji: kodomotachi ni ringo o futatsu zutsu agemashita.
examples.english: I gave the children two apples each.

examples.japanese: 毎日少しずつ漢字を覚えています。
examples.reading: まいにちすこしずつかんじをおぼえています。
examples.romaji: mainichi sukoshi zutsu kanji o oboete imasu.
examples.english: I'm learning kanji a little at a time every day.

examples.japanese: 一人ずつ部屋に入ってください。
examples.reading: ひとりずつへやにはいってください。
examples.romaji: hitori zutsu heya ni haitte kudasai.
examples.english: Please come into the room one at a time.

mistake.wrong: 学生ずつ本を一冊もらいました。
mistake.problem: ずつ follows the quantity that is repeated, not the people it is shared among.
mistake.right: 学生は本を一冊ずつもらいました。

entries.title: What should I do? You just need to…
entries.meaning: V-たらいい／V-ばいい: asks for advice (どうしたらいいですか, "what should I do?") or gives it ("you just need to V").
entries.when: Use it with a question word to ask for advice: 駅までどうやって行ったらいいですか, "how should I get to the station?"; 何を持っていけばいいですか. As an answer, it gives advice, often "all you need to do is": このボタンを押せばいいです. It can also express a hope: 晴れたらいいですね.
entries.why: The conditional (たら or ば) sets up "if you do V", and いい judges it: "if you do V, it will be good". So どうしたらいい asks "if I do what, will it be good?", the natural way to ask for advice in Japanese. As an answer it says V is enough for a good result, so it often means "you only have to". たら and ば are largely interchangeable here; たらいい is a little more conversational. With the past, ばよかった, the same shape becomes regret.

formation.note: 行ったらいい, したらいい. Polite いいですか／いいです.
行けばいい, すればいい.

formation.form: Question word … たら／ばいいですか
formation.note: どうしたらいいですか, 何を持っていけばいいですか.

examples.japanese: 駅までどうやって行ったらいいですか。
examples.reading: えきまでどうやっていったらいいですか。
examples.romaji: eki made dō yatte ittara ii desu ka.
examples.english: How should I get to the station?

examples.japanese: 「何を持っていけばいいですか。」「飲み物だけ持ってくればいいですよ。」
examples.reading: 「なにをもっていけばいいですか。」「のみものだけもってくればいいですよ。」
examples.romaji: "nani o motte ikeba ii desu ka." "nomimono dake motte kureba ii desu yo."
examples.english: "What should I bring?" "You only need to bring something to drink."

examples.japanese: わからないときは、先生に聞けばいいです。
examples.reading: わからないときは、せんせいにきけばいいです。
examples.romaji: wakaranai toki wa, sensei ni kikeba ii desu.
examples.english: When you don't understand, just ask the teacher.

mistake.wrong: 駅まで、どうやって行ってもいいですか。
mistake.problem: Meant as "how should I get to the station?". てもいいですか asks for permission. To ask how you should do something, use たらいい or ばいい.
mistake.right: 駅まで、どうやって行ったらいいですか。

distinguish_from.note: ばよかった looks back with regret. ばいい gives advice about what to do.
たらどうですか offers a suggestion to the listener. たらいい is mostly used to ask for advice, or to say what is enough.
といい is mainly a hope. たらいい and ばいい are mainly advice, though たらいい can also hope.

review.note: といいですか (何を持っていくといいですか) is also used to ask for advice; the entry leaves it out. Is that right for N4?

entries.title: It seems, it appears (judging from evidence)
entries.meaning: Plain form + ようだ／ようです: "it seems that…", "it looks as if…"; a conclusion drawn from evidence.
entries.when: Use it when you conclude something from what you have seen, heard or noticed: 電気が消えています。誰もいないようです, "the lights are off; it seems nobody's there". It is a little more formal than みたい, and common in careful speech and writing.
entries.why: よう means "appearance, likeness". ようだ says "it has the look of…": the speaker has some evidence and draws a conclusion, without stating it as certain. So it is less sure than はず, which reasons from known facts to what must be, and unlike stem + そう it is not limited to how something looks. It joins like a noun: の after a noun (休みのようだ), な after a な-adjective (静かなようだ), and plain forms after verbs and い-adjectives.

formation.form: Verb / い-adjective (plain form) + ようだ
formation.note: いないようだ, 降ったようだ, 忙しいようだ.

formation.form: な-adjective + な + ようだ; Noun + の + ようだ
formation.note: 静かなようだ, 休みのようだ. Polite ようです.

examples.japanese: 電気が消えています。誰もいないようです。
examples.reading: でんきがきえています。だれもいないようです。
examples.romaji: denki ga kiete imasu. dare mo inai yō desu.
examples.english: The lights are off. It seems nobody's there.

examples.japanese: 道がぬれています。夜の間に雨が降ったようです。
examples.reading: みちがぬれています。よるのあいだにあめがふったようです。
examples.romaji: michi ga nurete imasu. yoru no aida ni ame ga futta yō desu.
examples.english: The road is wet. It seems it rained during the night.

examples.japanese: 田中さんは今日は忙しいようです。
examples.reading: たなかさんはきょうはいそがしいようです。
examples.romaji: tanaka-san wa kyō wa isogashii yō desu.
examples.english: Tanaka-san seems to be busy today.

examples.japanese: この店は、日曜日は休みのようです。
examples.reading: このみせは、にちようびはやすみのようです。
examples.romaji: kono mise wa, nichiyōbi wa yasumi no yō desu.
examples.english: It looks like this shop is closed on Sundays.

mistake.wrong: あの人は学生ようです。
mistake.problem: After a noun, よう needs の.
mistake.right: あの人は学生のようです。

distinguish_from.note: みたい means the same, is more conversational, and joins nouns and な-adjectives directly (学生みたい).
そう after a stem is an impression from appearance, before you know. ようだ is a conclusion from evidence of any kind.
はず reasons from known facts to what should be so. ようだ concludes from what you observe, less firmly.
